Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Did you end up with a career completely unrelated to your undergraduate major?
Answer: Regular readers of mine will know at least the outline of the story: I majored in history and English as an undergraduate, became a software developer, and am now a computer scientist. I’ve written the story a few times, but now I intend to pin this answer. I only have one regret about majors, and it’s not what most people expect. I originally wanted to major in microbiology, but I was talked out of that because micro was in the college of agriculture. I was swayed by bigotry. I luckily landed a computer lab job in sophomore year, after years of food service. I hung out with CS majors, learned HTML (when this was a rare skill), and learned a bit of scripting. I took one CS course as a gen ed in my last semester, and fell in love. Some self-study and a bit of luck and I landed my first software development job. I then realized that it would help to have a credential. One of my mentors (a studio art major) had started a part-time software engineering MS program, and on his advice, I started the program. It took 3.5 years to finish, but I was not in a rush. By the end of the MS, I was tired of software development and wanted to find something new. I was really excited about research in CS, so I went for a PhD… and now I’m a CS professor (well, assistant professor). Please let me know if you want more detail about any part. Thanks Smit Dagli for encouraging me to write this in a place I can find it.

Question: I’m currently studying software engineering at university, and I’m thinking of changing my major to data science and artificial intelligence. Any advice?

Students studying data science should take additional statistics and if linear algebra isn't required for the CS degree, they should study that, too. Both of these will be beneficial for computer science students, too. As for an AI major, I'd need to see the details; there might be some neuroscience or symbolic reasoning coursework, some of which might be interesting. Overall difference? Minimal. Nor will it impact your job opportunities; the tech industry hires by skills, not by majors. More broadly, I completely agree with Dani; we are in an AI summer, but every summer has been followed by a winter so far.

Question: Is it possible to do a different bachelor program after a first one before pursuing a master’s in a European or American university?
Answer: Absolutely, you can do this in the United States. There are two problems. First, most of the universities you've heard of will not accept students for a second bachelors degree; even without those students, they have too many applicants, so this is a perfectly reasonable thing for those universities to do. Second, you will need to spend at least $30,000 a year, and probably for about three years. If you want to pursue a degree in a location you will be more excited by, it can get much, much more expensive. And this is for the bachelor's degree; the master's degree will be two years on top of that.

Question: Is Trump likely to be nominated as a Supreme Court judge if Republicans win the White House in 2028?
Answer: Let’s ignore for a moment that Trump has no legal training (while not required, but the last justice appointed without a legal education was James Byrne in 1941, and he had read law and was admitted to the bar). In June of 2029, Trump will turn 83 years. The oldest person appointed to SCOTUS in history was Horace Lurton, who was 65 when he was appointed associate justice. (Harlan Stone was 68 when he was appointed chief justice, but he had already served for more than a decade as an associate justice.) In this hypothetical scenario, the Democratic Party would be quite pleased to confirm Trump if they held the Senate. He is unlikely to be more conservative than an alternate selection, and his tenure on the court is likely to be short. OK, they’d fight his confirmation tooth-and-nail as a matter of principle, but that would not be in their best interest.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Why are many universities so classist when they have whole sociology departments dedicated toward 'deconstructing' classism?
Answer: Wow, OK, let’s see what we need to unpack here. I get what you’re getting at, but we need to reconsider some things taken at face value. First, there are sociologists who claim that they are deconstructing things. Jacques Derrida would be furious with their misuse of the concept (and then probably find it hilarious), but he’s dead, so they can get away with it. Most sociologists aren’t deconstructing anything; there’s much more to sociology than poor applications of postmodern French philosophy. Second, universities are inherently and inevitably “classist” because they reinforce the haves and the have-nots. When run properly, they move some people from have-nots to the haves, but the system is reinforced intentionally. No one is genuinely trying to upend society from a university faculty position. Some small number want to be perceived that way. Third, one of my favorite undergrad professors had this to say about faculty (I’m paraphrasing): faculty are basically all middle class and hold bourgeois values, but some of us don’t want to be and try to project either upper-class or working-class values and identities. It’s a performative identity; we’re still all trying to pay for our houses, keep our cars running, save for retirement, etc. It seems like every few years, we get a new “de-” or an “anti-” that’s fashionable among a very vocal group of academics. So far, none of the “de-” or “anti-” movements have changed academia, let alone society. I’m not certain that they’re intended to.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I made a fool of myself by getting high in front of my graduate school peers. How do I recover from this?
Answer: So I’ve had some experience with embarrassment. It turns out that some people are more sensitive to embarrassment than others, to the point where what one person would look back on with mild amusement might cause another person to struggle to engage. First, I’m sure that you’ve been told that other people will not even remember the incident, and that’s often true. Second, you’re allowed to be human in front of other people. You’re allowed to make mistakes and errors in judgment. Some warrant apologies (less commonly than I once believed), some warrant learning the lesson to not repeat, and some could have consequences, but nobody will take away your human being card on the basis of having gotten high, even if you did something embarrassing. Third, if you genuinely have harmed your reputation, then the solution is not to disengage. It’s also not usually a good idea to apologize; you apologize if you harm other people. The best solution is to display a more even temperament. It’s rare that a reputation is destroyed in an instant, and it generally requires something much more severe than some embarrassing or foolish behavior in an evening. I remember one of my first professional jobs. There was a guy, Tom G. Man, I hated that jerk. He would antagonize me. He was arrogant and obnoxious. I was trying to be professional, and he was the least professional person in the office. Then one day I had had enough of the job and of him and I yelled and kicked a small garbage can across the room. I was furious. Tom laughed, and said something of the general form of, “OK, so you are a human being.” I was (and still am) wound a little tightly. After that point, we were friends; he was a genuinely nice guy who actually did me a huge favor, helping me not take the job or the world too seriously. It’s a lesson I have to remind myself of regularly. I just found him on LinkedIn and sent him a connection request. Anyway, people like human beings. They don’t like people who don’t let their defects show. They see people like that as arrogant, even if that’s not accurate.

Question: How do I make a strong profile to get a fully funded scholarship?
Answer: It is nearly impossible for US students to guarantee that they will get fully-funded scholarships, outside of a handful of states that offer full tuition scholarships to public colleges and universities to in-state students with high grades. Florida, New York, and Louisiana have such programs. Note that these do not cover living expenses, which are often higher than tuition. However, the student can use federal aid for that, if they qualify. An increasing number of states (including California) also offer community college to all or most students for free. Students who have very strong academic records can often get a large merit scholarship from an institution where they would be in the top 10% of students (typically measured on GPA, SAT, or both). Based on your profile and question, I assume that you are an international student. For international students, it’s almost impossible to get comprehensive aid to cover all or the vast majority of costs. You should expect to spend at least $30,000 per year to study in the US, and more if you want to attend an institution you’ve heard of or that’s in a more exciting area of the country. If you are one of the best students in your nation, then you should have local assistance in pursuing admission to a university that will fund you. If not, your best bet is Berea College, which offers full tuition scholarships to all students, but they only admit students with demonstrated need and they only admit about 30 international students per year.

Question: My Jr. Year GPA in high school is 3.7, but freshman and sophomore’s GPA is only 3.1. Do I have a chance to get into a public college in California?
Answer: If you reside in California, you are effectively guaranteed a seat at least one CSU. You have no realistic chance of admission to any UC other than UC Merced. Cal Poly SLO and Cal Poly Pomona are almost certainly off the table, too. Realistically, you probably have access to at least ten CSU schools, even if you are not from California, although the cost will be high if you aren’t. And of course you have access to community colleges, too. You should visit a couple of CSU campuses and your local community college and decide which ones seem like fit for you. Apply to a few different CSUs, see where you get in, and make a final decision. If you do choose to attend a community college, which can be a great decision if it’s the best fit, make sure you register early; classes can fill quickly, so even though you could walk in the day before classes begin and register, you won’t get good choices.

Question: How/why did Intel lose its way against competitors such as Arm, AMD, and Nvidia? Is Intel, despite its vast resources, simply unable to deliver technology that matches its competitors?
Answer: Honestly, the industry backed them into a corner. More than two decades ago, they tried to retire the x86 platform. Admittedly, Itanium (IA-64, which yes, was started by HP, but Intel ended up the larger partner) wasn’t great, but it had a lot of potential that never saw the light of day. x86 was just entrenched. A few things happened in the mid 2000s that locked Intel onto rails. First, AMD presented a strong modernization/extension of x86 into 64-bit computing; Intel had spent a fortune on Itanium, and implementing IP from another company was far less expensive than developing their own (and seen as a little bit of payback). Second, they shifted to multicore, which dramatically extended the life of the x86 platform. Third, POWER abandoned the consumer market and Apple abandoned POWER for the x86; Intel and AMD basically own the laptop, desktop, and vast majority of the server market. Fourth, Intel’s M-series processors… well, they sucked. People will occasionally say something like, “they should’ve started a skunk Works too…”, And I’m quite sure they did. I’m equally certain that whatever was proposed was shot down as being a threat to their core market. As the 900 pound gorilla in the room, yes, Intel had outsized influence, but the problem is that 900 pound gorillas are not very flexible. Their momentum carries them in certain directions, and there is a huge incentive to change… until the tables turn and rather than dangerous, change becomes necessary. Thus is ever the evolution and history of technology companies. Mostly. IBM quite cleverly (mostly) got out of the hardware game before it would have collapsed on them, but they were literally ridiculed for giving that up.

Question: If I complete two years at a community college can I transfer to another community college to get better grades?
Answer: As others indicate, there are a number of things wrong with your plan. First and foremost, transferring won’t improve your grades. You need a specific, concrete plan to improve your grades, and you have to enact that plan over course of time. Even with thst plan , it’s difficult to get higher grades. Second, community colleges exist to prepare students for vocational careers (e.g., dental hygienist) or for transfer to a four-year college or university to complete a bachelors degree. I assume you are on the latter track. You should complete your associate’s degree as quickly as possible and transfer. Some four year colleges and universities transfer grades, and some don’t. It might seem compelling to earn some higher grades before transferring if the four-year college you plan to attend does transfer grades, but GPA doesn’t matter very much. Employers don’t care, and grad programs will Consider dramatically changed performance. Third, all four-year institutions will look at all of your transcripts. If you want to demonstrate higher grades, you can do so at your community college. It won’t help you to have earned lower grades at community college and then have earned higher grades at community college B any more than it will help to stay at community college A and start earning higher grades.

Question: I get low GPA because ADHD and Asperger's and depression have severely affected my cognition. And my GPA after graduation is 2.9, what should I do if I apply to the university? Do I need to take too much Ritalin?
Answer: I can't speak to outside of the United States, but in the US, 2.9 GPA is more than sufficient to get accepted to many colleges and universities. They will not be among the most competitive, but regardless of the reason, you have not demonstrated the ability to perform at that level. It doesn't really matter much, because what is taught in a college classroom sets a lower bound, not upper bound. you can and should learn more than what is taught. That's what experiential learning is all about. Rather than jumping to taking stimulants, I would recommend finding a therapist who works with people with ADHD, ASD, and depression. They may direct you to a physician who prescribes medication, but they can also help you develop skills to manage the symptoms. There are several colleges and universities in the US that specialize in working with neurodivergent students. However, most of them tend to be fairly expensive; if you can afford the cost, great. Like all colleges and universities, you actually have to investigate your specific situation with them, rather than just look at the list price. The average cost of a private college university is less than half of the list cost, but your cost may be even significantly below that. The one I know the most of is Landmark College; they tend to try to mainstream students into traditional four-year institutions after two years, which is what I like about them.

Question: What should I do? I want to join a program where I can become a respiratory therapist but the whole tuition cost is 41k with everything included. Is it worth it? Moreover, I have to take out loans for it?
Answer: From the perspective of somebody in California, that doesn't seem like a good deal. Like many clinical healthcare programs offered at the associate's degree level, this is really a three-year program. You'll need at least a year to complete the college level-prerequisites, then you have to apply to the program (toward the end of your first year), and admission is competitive. However, the tuition costs will be minimal, certainly nothing like $41,000. Community college can be much more expensive in other states, but look at your local community colleges and see if they offer a program. Many students find what you're finding, which is that private trade schools are very expensive, even compared to traditional colleges, especially on a per-year cost. If your choice is between this program and nothing, then it's not unreasonable to take out some loans. Be aware that $41,000 is more than the average student takes out to complete a four-year degree (significantly more). It is also more than the federal government will lend you, so this means getting private loans, and you need to carefully review the terms. Interest rates are high right now, but they'll hopefully go down before you start the program, at community college or this school.

Question: What are some important things to know before learning Python/C++/Java/etc. as a beginner programmer?
Answer: First, don’t try to learn multiple languages as once. Second, choose Java. Python is much, much easier to start, but you’ll build some bad habits and you won’t learn about typing (as in data types, not pressing keys on a keyboard) and other middle-level programming concerns. But more than that, Java’s error message is very clear, very precise, and completely unambiguous. If you get an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, you know that you have access an invalid index in an array. No, you don’t know what that means now, but you will. And you’ll always get the same error from the same bad code. That isn’t necessarily true of C or C++. Why are error messages so important? Because you code will constantly be full of errors. Which is why thing number three to remember is that persistence is essential. When you’ll spend far more time dealing with errors than writing code.

Question: Can you get a “movie-like” university life in Arkansas?
Answer: Sure. Well, I guess it depends somewhat on what you mean by “movie-like”, but Arkansas has a number of colleges and universities, some of which will likely be appealing to you. In fact, fellow Quoran Gabriel J. Ferrer is a faculty member at Hendrix College. While I didn’t visit the campus, I was interested in Hendrix when I was looking at colleges. It has a strong reputation and while it’s expensive compared to public options, it’s less expensive than many other similar small, private liberal arts colleges. I’m not going to claim that Arkansas is the bright, shining center of the US. It’s one of the poorest states in the US, which is a big part of the reason why it has some of the worst public school metrics in the US. But even considering that, there will be excellent students and teachers in K-12, and the same for colleges and universities. I don’t know much about the University of Arkansas, but it’s a big, public university with a long football tradition and what looks to be a nice and fairly standard campus. While it’s far from a perfect measure, one way of evaluating universities is to see if they ever have Rhodes Scholars. It’s a measure of “will I be around brilliant. ambitious people.” Arkansas has had 11 over the years, with the most recent in 2022. But since you wrote “university life”, I assume you are not from the US. Even in relatively poor state like Arkansas, international students should expect to spend no less than $30,000 per year for their education.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can I do Aeronautical or Aerospace Engineering at university without Further Maths at A-Levels? I’m going with Maths, Physics, Chemistry and economics in A-Levels so far.
Answer: There are only about 130 universities in the UK, IIRC, and most of them will not offer aeronautical or aerospace engineering. You can look at each course and see what they require. However, I have to wonder why you are not taking Further Maths and why you are taking four A-levels. My understanding is that Further Maths is an accelerated/deeper version of Maths, and that there isn’t much reason for a fourth A level. You need to talk to someone who knows you and the educational system in the UK at a more detailed level, but those seem like decisions to revisit.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Are there scholarships for international students at Georgia Tech? How competitive are they? What do I need to be eligible/apply?
Answer: This is something you should be able to find on your own. There are two large scholarships (in terms of money): Stamps President’s Scholars and Gold Scholars, and spoiler, only US citizens and permanent residents, UK citizens, or in some cases citizens of the Republic of Ireland are considered. Public colleges and universities rarely award scholarships of any size to international students. On the contrary, international students are sources of funding for universities, since they pay full tuition, which is much more than state residents pay.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Do you think higher education is a tool to control people?
Answer: Look, you can stretch the definition enough that anything is a tool to control people. We tell students what to do and if they don’t do those things, there are consequences. But the worst consequence is we say “Go away, we’re done with you.” There are professors who will insist that students mimic back their (the professor’s) views. They’ve turned the classroom into a bully pulpit, with emphasis on “bully”. I used to believe that such claims were false. I was wrong. But they aren’t as common as critics would have you believe. And some internet pundits have objected to my own radical agenda that students in the classroom must treat each other with respect. That’s apparently a bridge too far for some. For the vast majority of interactions and experiences, higher education is a system to educate people. And the vast majority of people who carry through on the program will benefit financially and intellectually. There are very few ways to invest in yourself that are as effective as higher education. But the people who are using it as a bully pulpit… that’s not OK. If your professor is forcing you to actually attest to a viewpoint, to make political actions outside of the class, to hate, you should not be exposed to that. The single best thing you can do is to push back. File complaints, drop classes, contact FIRE, and write letters or editorials in your school newspaper. One of the problems with academia is that we often don’t know what’s happening in another person’s class. Make sure that is not the case.[1]

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How good is the idea to take a student loan to pay for a portion (not all) of the tuition at certain universities in the US?
Answer: This could be anywhere from a wonderful idea to a terrible idea. I recall reading a few years ago about a young woman who had graduated (maybe around 2015?) rom Northern Ohio University with $100,000 in debt. She majored in English (which is fine) and had done no career preparation (which is not fine). That’s a bad decision. I also remember a student of mine who finally faced facts that she couldn’t live in her parents’ chaotic house and commute an hour each way, each day and actually graduate on time, so taking out a few thousand dollars (actually for living expenses, not tuition) was a life-altering my good idea. That first young woman was ill-advised. In fact, unless there are pieces I don’t know about, I think that situation is reprehensible, and yes, I blame the university. I dread to think of what might’ve happened to that second young woman. I can’t recall her name at the moment, but last I remember, she was working as a consultant for Microsoft. I don’t think she regretted taking on a few thousand dollars in debt. So… anywhere between “taking those loans will cripple you financially, possibly for decades” to “not taking those loans will derail a professional career and high income.” Most choices will be between. But whatever you do to pay for college, you need to start career prep ASAP.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: If aeronautical engineering isn't an option, could I settle for mechanical and after I graduate, learn what I missed from aeronautical on my own (aerodynamics, fluid dynamics, etc.) and have a successful career with that.?
Answer: If you want to be a working engineer, you need two things: a degree in engineering, and your first engineering job. Once you have both of those things, it becomes easier to get experience and move around and between industries, especially if you are very competitive (in the sense of being excellent at your job, very hardworking, and willing to network). Many engineers working in the aerospace industry have degrees in mechanical engineering, because they're working on mechanical systems. The same as true for electrical engineering and electronics systems. I cannot stress enough the importance of networking. Many young people, especially those in fields like engineering that tend to attract introverts, think that if they work hard in classes and internships, it can make up for their unwillingness to network. Newsflash: it can't. If you want to be in a highly specialized field with a limited number of jobs(like aerospace engineering), you must be willing to network. This is true regardless of the degree you have. Personally, I find networking to be incredibly uncomfortable and stressful, but I do it successfully because it's that important. I wouldn't have my career if I wasn't willing to network. Like any other set of skills, it's something you build on gradually; you don't need to be the best person at networking tomorrow. You just work at it regularly. There are countless online resources in how to work effectively.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do I get into a university in America as an undergrad, when I am not an American citizen and graduated from a third world country? I was born in Iraq and came to America when I was 4 I lived in America for 10 years before returning back to Iraq.
Answer: Honestly, it's just a question of money. If you have enough money ($30,000 to $100,000 per year), there are colleges and universities in the United States that will admit you. If you don't have enough money, you have to hope to get a scholarship, and they are very, very few of these. You may wish to look at Berea College, which offers scholarships to all admitted students; I think they admit about 30 students from outside the US per year. All applicants must have demonstrated financial need (which they will explain in the application materials). Beyond that, if you have some evidence that you are one of the best students in your year in all of Iraq, like major national and international awards, you might be competitive for a full scholarship in the US. You should seek out guidance from people in your home country.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can I directly email professors of the university I want to apply to in the USA asking for a recommendation?
Answer: If you are applying for an undergraduate (bachelor's degree) program, there's no point. Even if a professor would be willing to recommend you, they won't have any impact in the admission process. If you are applying to a PhD program, in most cases this is a complete waste of time. I have been told there are some fields where this is normal. You need advice from somebody at your current institution or in your country who has experience with helping people get into graduate programs in the US. But let me tell you my own experience as a professor in the United States. I occasionally get emails from international students who want to work on a graduate degree with me. These emails are full of praise for my research. There are two core problems with this. First, I'm not an incredibly productive researcher, and it's very obvious that these students have no idea what my research consists of, anyway. Second, my university does not offer any graduate degrees in computer science. We may be starting up a master's degree, but it wouldn't be funded for international students. We will never have a PhD program we are statutorily prohibited from offering a PhD. My understanding is that, in some countries, a fawning email full of praise and adoration, combined with offer to work very hard, might open a door or an opportunity. The United States doesn't work like that. If you want to apply to any academic program in the United States, the most important thing is to put together a good application. You should have competitive grades and exam scores (as relevant), combined with a strong personal statement indicating why you are seeking this education and what you plan to do with it, and letters of recommendation from people who actually know you and who can speak to your specific qualifications.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What happens if I have to repeat a year at a university?
Answer: In the United States, that doesn't really happen. You take multiple courses in any given year, and you can pass or fail each course. If you pass, you don't need to retake it, but if you fail, you do need to retake the course, at least if it's required for your degree. If you failed all of your courses in a year, you would be suspended academically and would be unlikely to return to that university. A fair number of students need to take an additional semester, usually because of taking relatively few credits, withdrawing from courses, needing to repeat courses because of low grades, or changing/deciding a major late in this process. For them, they must pay an additional semester of living expenses and an additional semester of tuition, but that's not usually the end of the world. If you need more than one additional semester, that's a good sign you've dug yourself a bit of a hole. There are certainly legitimate circumstances (e.g., major health crises) that would justify needing an extra year, and an extra year is fairly common and nit really concerning in engineering (the coursework is that heavy), but if you just dawdled or underperformed academically, you've increased the cost of your education by about 25% and given up a year of income and career progression. This also isn't the end of the world, but it's time to start thinking about what's going wrong and why.

Question: How do I convince my parents that streaming is my job? I have a sizeable fanbase (I get recognized in the game I play, get donos, etc) and make sure to spend time off-stream helping them (Basically everything) but they don't think it's a "real" job
Answer: If your rising bank balance doesn't convince your parents, there are two possibilities. The first is that nothing will convince your parents, so it's not worth worrying about. The second is that your bank balance isn't rising all that quickly, in which case your parents have a point; you may have some income from streaming, but if you can't make a living off of it, it's a closer to a hobby than a job. At best we might call it a side gig, but then what's the main gig its alongside of? If you can show projections for income increases that aren't based on hope, that might help you, but… lots of people want to be streamers as their career. Lots of people get to the point where they're getting a little bit of money. Lots of people get a little bit of fame. The percentage of those who get traction, like you, who will ever actually make a living off of this is minuscule.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What TV show was unwatchable at first but became amazing for you later on?
Answer: I watched the pilot of Firefly. It’s a science fiction show in the style of a Western. The pilot made no sense, I was missing too many pieces, and it just seemed like a showpiece of a Western-style heist, complete with betrayal. But (as fans will angrily have noted), I didn’t see the pilot. It was presented as the pilot, but this wasn’t the first episode. Fox (?) thought that this was the episode that would go over best the with audience. They were wrong. I think I watched one other episode, but I recall the first leaving a bad taste in my mouth, so I probably wasn’t prepared to enjoy it Later, after the movie came out, a friend convinced me to watch the show. She loaned me DVDs of the show and the movie. Watched from the beginning, the show made sense, and the true first episode set up a lot of intrigue that would carry interest in the show. Firefly was cancelled after half a season. A big push to bring the show back eventually led to a film being greenlit. The film didn’t prove much more popular than the show, and probably was a losing enterprise for the studio. But fans got closure, and it’s really quite the ride. What would have happened had Fox run episodes in order, promoted the show properly, etc? I don’t know. While fans are rabid and I do think it’s one of the best (short) seasons of television, I’m not convinced that it would have been big. In fact, I doubt it would have been long-lived, which I’m not too upset about. And here’s where I further disagree with fans; I don’t think there should have been (much) more. There are 14 episodes, including the 90-minute (real) pilot and 13 45-minute episodes, and a two-hour movie. Roughly speaking, about 19 hours of content. In recent years, we’ve seen that “limited series” of this length and even shorter can pack quite a punch with little or no filler (not that all achieve that). I think if she show had taken four years to meander to and through the events of the movie, there would have been a lot of filler. Between Buffy the Vampire Slayer and its spinoff, Angel, Whedon and others milked over 250 episodes, most of it filler; great for true fans, but not so great to slog through if you weren’t already a huge fan. His later show, Dollhouse, only got two seasons, and it was a great ride. As it was, there was only one episode that I didn’t enjoy (“Heart of Gold”).

Question: Do you have to pay FAFSA Pell Grant back if you drop out at the end of the year (in case a good business opportunity arises)?
Answer: Mark Kantrowitz wrote an excellent answer on this.[1] First, it’s important to note that FAFSA (a form) and the Pell grant (federal financial aid for higher education) are two separate things. You will find the answer you are looking for by searching for information on the Pell grant, not about FAFSA. That’s why these distinctions are important. There is no such thing as FAFSA aid. Second, as Mark’s answer states, you need to complete 60% of the term (semester, quarter, etc., whatever your college uses) in order to be eligible for federal financial aid, and most specifically the Pell grant. As you presumably know, grants aren’t paid back, but if you withdraw from college without completing the term, you may have to repay all or part of the money. To the best of my understanding, the college returns the aid to the federal government, and the student must repay lost aid to the college. However, I’m not 100% certain of that.

Question: Is medical imaging demanded? What are the countries that have the highest demand for this degree? Is this degree worth it and does it pay well?
Answer: So… medical imaging in the US is in demand. Almost everyone has to enter the career the same way: an associate of applied science in medical imagining. These programs typically take three years and they are competitive. But there isn’t sufficient demand that this can be the basis of coming to the US for employment. Typically you need a bachelor’s degree to even be considered for an H-1B for any professional career. The costs of an H-1B visa are high enough that they don’t make sense to employ a medical imaging tech.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Should I take any AP classes in my sophomore year? I just moved to NYC.
Answer: No. I have seen some statements that AP Human Geography is valuable for some HS sophomores, but think about it this way: should high school sophomores be ready for college-level courses? Outside of a small and obvious group (AP Calc, Bio, Chem, Physics, maybe US History), I don’t see much actual value in AP courses or exams. You should take a few in your junior year to demonstrate the ability to work hard, but far too many HS students (and their parents) think that AP is far more important/profound than it really is. Now, there is an exception to this. If your HS offers general college-prep, honors, and AP courses and the honors course is paced too slow, or if they only offer general college-prep and AP courses and the general college-prep courses are too slow, then take the AP course, but just take it as an accelerated course. Don’t obsess over the idea that it’s a college-level course. It may be, but that’s not saying much about college-level general education courses these days.

Question: Is there any organization who gives study loan to international students for masters degree in USA?
Answer: Not really, no. At least, not within the US. If you had a US relative, they might be willing to co-sign a loan from a US bank, but that basically means that they are borrowing the money for you. There’s another problem: getting an F-1 visa. Having a loan based in the US is the exact opposite of what you want, especially if a relative is a co-signer. It’s an incentive to stay in the US, and if the visa officer isn’t convinced you plan to leave the US at the end your degree (including OPT/CPT, but nothing beyond), they will deny your visa. You must have financial resources to pay for one year of educational and living expenses to secure a visa. There may be banks or other organizations in your home country. There is the Fulbright Scholars program, which will pay for your master’s degree, but that’s incredibly competitive.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How would you advise me to choose a degree? I currently want to do research, and have a Bachelor of Science degree.
Answer: I would advise you to not choose a degree. I would advise you at this point to choose a career. A specific career in a specific field. Unfortunately, it’s not sufficient to choose to “do research”. There are many types of jobs that fall into that category, and then there’s the whole matter of what you’re researching. Start with MyNextMove, a free tool from the US Department of Labor. After completing the interest inventory, record your scores somewhere (so you can easily go back) and then look at careers in Zones 4 & 5. Choose one specific career and explore it for a few weeks. Join a professional organization. Reach out to alumni from your institution who are in that role. Verify that there is demand, and what you would need to do to enter the career. See if it’s a fit. If so, proceed with what you need to do in order to enter. If not, choose another career until you find one to commit to.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Apart from language and numerical (mathematics) literacy, is it necessary to have programming (algorithms) literacy lessons in schools?
Answer: Let me re-ask your question in plain terms, and this will be the version of the question I am answering: what should all school students know about algorithms? Teaching algorithms isn't new, specific computer science, or even specific to mathematics. Any step wise process to solve a problem is an algorithm. Like many other faculty, I often start my introductory computer science course by having students make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. I stand in front of the room with a plate, a knife, an unopened jar of peanut butter, an unopened jar of jelly, and an unopened loaf of bread. I asked them to give me instructions, and I follow the instructions to the letter. It turns out that it's very hard to explain to somebody how to make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich if they don't know how to do most of the tasks. It's also pretty funny, so it's a memorable lesson. is this one thing I wish I had known earlier, it's that, within mathematics, there are multiple ways to perform/solve arithmetic problems. I'm not saying that I wasn't taught this, but if I was, I don't remember it. My understanding of mathematics really advanced when I truly understood and appreciated the definition of a function (which I can guarantee you was not the first time it was presented to me). A function is just a relationship between two sets, called the domain and co-domain. In more concrete terms, a function is just a way of relating some kind of output value to every valid input value. But that's too advanced for early days in school. Have you ever seen these videos of students (mostly in Asia) performing multi-column multiplication using crossed lines? If done correctly and practiced well, it's much, much faster than the method I was taught. In practical terms, that's pointless; this is why we have calculators. I also think the method we are taught leads to a better understanding; the crossed lines method is more of a party trick. But I think it would be valuable to show students this method, have them practice it a bit, and then show them why it leads to the same result as other methods. Beyond that, I remain skeptical about teaching much about computer science in grade school. With rare exception, I see children walk away from these lessons having learned only that computer can be made to do things. In the old days, we would've added in that computers were pretty neat, but students experience computers regularly. I'm not saying it's necessarily bad idea, but I have yet to really understand the value proposition. I am much more supportive of focusing on the Three Rs (an old American colloquialism for reading, writing, and arithmetic) than on adding more topics to the core curriculum, at least through eighth grade, but realistically through high school, too.

Question: I'm considering submitting a literature review paper to the User Modeling and User-Adapted interaction (UMUAI) journal. Does anyone know the current acceptance rate for this journal? Also, do they typically accept review papers?

Question: Can a 25-year-old apply to college in the USA without a high school diploma and 10th grade certificate as an international student?
Answer: There are two separate issues here. The first is admission to a college, and the second is a visa. Kim's answer is the closest to mine. I have no doubt that there are community colleges that will admit you, but you will bear the full costs (starting at $25,000 a year when you include all expenses, but most will be more expensive). Even if you have the money, though, visa officers may be concerned. Most students who start college without a secondary credential (e.g., a high school diploma) will need to take remedial coursework. Community colleges offer this (generally speaking), but it's unclear why an international student would come to the US and spend a lot of money to complete the equivalent of a high school education.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Which university do you think would be better for an undergraduate chemical engineering degree, Monash or University of Edinburgh? Which would open up more opportunities?
Answer: Education is local, so broadly speaking, opportunities in the UK will be much better if you go to Edinburgh, and they will be much better in Australia if you go to Monash. Assuming costs are similar and reasonable, I recommend that you follow the British maxim "start as you mean to go on "and attend the university in the country where you want to be after. That having been said, I think the most striking difference between the two is where they are located. While they are both located in capital cities, the two cities are quite different (at least in how they present, as I've never been to either). Melbourne is the larger (approximate metro population of 5 million vs. not even 1 million in Edinburgh) and younger (dating to the 1830s if we only speak about colonial settlement, vs. at least 900 years for Edinburgh). Monash was founded in 1958, vs the University of Edinburgh, which dates to 1583. Edinburgh will also be much cooler, wetter, and more gray. For me personally, I can quickly identify that, due to city age, climate, and population size, I'm much more likely to enjoy living in Edinburgh or three years or so, and while I have contemplated spending extended time in the UK, I have not done so far Australia. But that's me; my point is that my preferences matter for my decisions, and yours should matter for you.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Should I become an LPC or an LMFT? I have always been interested in marriage counseling, but I don't know which route I should take.
Answer: So there will be some differences in coursework and your clinical supervised work. Psychological counselors focus on working with an individual, often somebody with a diagnosed mental health disorder, while marriage and family therapists focus on working with couples and families, who don't typically have diagnosed disorders. But while some family dysfunction can be tied to circumstances, understanding how people can differ and/or struggle in dealing with problems will be beneficial, and some of the people you will be working with will have diagnosed or undiagnosed mental health disorders. The therapist I've known have all stated consistently that, while their education provided them a strong background, they really learned how to work with people in the practice, which is why there's a long supervised clinical practice. I know that in California, an LMFT can work with individuals.[1] Certainly in my area, there is enough demand for either and even given the differences, I believe that the similarities and high demand mean that it would be possible to move from one to the other. I think LPC or LCSW might give you a bit more flexibility, but I think that's going to be very local. I strongly encourage you to find some mentors who have these degrees/licenses and ask them for guidance. Most people are willing to help out students from their alma mater so troll LinkedIn a bit (unless you know some people in the field), reach out to some people who are maybe between five and 10 years into their careers and see if you can meet them for coffee or something. Good luck!

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is it worth it to apply to medical school?
Answer: Probably not. The odds are against you. A significant majority of the people who apply to medical school and United States will never be accepted. That's the problem with pursuing something competitive; you entertain risk. If you can do so without feeling destroyed when/if you don't get what you're pursuing, go for it. If you can't deal with the loss that may come, then you shouldn't try. The Internet is filled with information (a lot of valuable, much of it crap) about how to get into medical school, but the short answer is that you must have a strong academic record generally, strong grades in the premed courses, and a strong MCAT score. After that, soft factors (volunteering in the medical community, demonstrating a desire to help in other types of activity, showing willingness to do hard work even when it's unpleasant) come into play. If your grades and MCAT score are high enough and you feel comfortable taking a risk, you may find yourself in a position thinking, "I can't not try." I think that's a good place to be mentally. If you don't get in, it's going to hurt. There's no way to avoid those emotions. But if you fail to get into med school, it's highly likely that your journey can lead you to the career that is going to work for you. Few people who were competitive for admission to medical school and didn't get in will end up working minimum wage jobs. But here's the kicker: there's a hidden risk. If you don't apply to medical school, that sets you on a pathway of not taking risks, which is a risk in itself. If you never take risks, you'll never fail, but you'll never succeed, either. At least, not in something compelling.

Question: Does studying MIS over CS hurt my chances of employment or possible future prospects academically and professionally?
Answer: Shane is correct; depending on the job you want pursue, one or the other will probably be better. I can tell you this: the MIS professors on the floor above me make more than I do. Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do I deal with a bad teacher AP Pre calc teacher? My teacher gave us a pop quiz and only gave us 10 minutes to do 6 questions. It gave anxiety and now im scared I will fail her class. Any advice anyone can provide me with?
Answer: I'm not sure I can add much value to what Melissa be wrote. As with others, I don't think this is a bad teacher, although it's normal for there to be pairings of teachers and students that don't mesh. Until I read the third sentence, I had thought to recommend switching to non-AP pre-calculus. The AP part isn't that big of a deal. However, if one pop quiz in one class gave you such severe anxiety that you're worried you will fail the class, you need to get some help dealing with your anxiety. That's the number one priority. Whether you switch to a different class or not, you need to talk to your parents and then talk to a doctor. Test anxiety goes away when the test is over (for the most part); it's just a phenomenon of anticipation and the testing experience itself. I'm obviously not qualified to diagnose what you're experiencing, but it's not test anxiety. Hopefully you know that you have nothing to worry about, and that even if you got a zero on this quiz, it says nothing about your final grade. Your teacher is likely trying to get you to work faster and yes, that's a real-world thing. That's why you need to get this taken care of now. You can bury your head in the sand, but it's not going to get any better until you get some support. I eventually learned to love the teachers and professors who pushed me the hardest, who cut me the least slack, and who demanded the best work of me, often on short timelines. However, that wasn't until I started to get comfortable with both my abilities and my limitations. Don't give up on this class and step back from judging the teacher. Even if you choose to switch to a different pre-class, seek out the treatment that's going to help you better cope with exams and classes and life events where you feel a lot of pressure. Good luck, and as a final message, I can promise you that when you start to work on this issue, it will get better.

Question: What can engineers do to manufacture an aircraft to carry 10k passengers? Why and how?
Answer: First, they would need to find 10,000 people who all wanted to go from one particular place to another at the same time. Even if we were to pick the most frequently flown route, that's a lot of people. Second, they would need to solve a fundamental industrial/human factors engineering problem: how do we efficiently load and unload 10,000 people from an aircraft? The answer is that we don't. It would take hours. This creates two problems: the aircraft is now completely impractical, and it could also never be certified for safety reasons. An emergency evacuation would take far too long.

Question: How might a HS Sophmore start a volunteer abroad program? I'd really like to give my classmates the chance to help out others in less developed countries. What might the costs and supplies look like? Any ideas of fundraisers to help out with money?
Answer: Money and connections. That's why these "volunteer abroad" programs only briefly had any impact on admission to the self-styled "elite" colleges and universities; they quickly realized that these were more functions of parents spending money than students really caring about digging Wells in South America or Africa. There are plenty of programs that will give you a volunteering abroad experience in exchange for a few thousand dollars. Whether the costs are legitimate or not, I don't know, but you will definitely travel to some other country and dig Wells or do something similar. Many churches have mission programs, some of which will involve students, but given the complexities of volunteering abroad and the tendency of young people to be… well, young people, you typically have to be involved for a long time. You don't necessarily have to be religious, I suppose, just involved in a mission group's work. What kind of costs would this require? Assuming you are connecting with an existing program, you can just act as a front. The costs are on the order of a few thousand dollars per student. If you genuinely want to build something new, I suspect it would require hundreds of thousands of dollars, plus connections. If your parents are involved in national government or international business, they can probably get you started. My suggestion is this. Pick something that you care about, and something related to your local community (construed broadly, so it could be your metro area). Then start volunteering. Once you start volunteering, recruit your friends to join you. Figure out how you as a group of young young people can have impact on your local community. raising a few thousand dollars great, but it's rarely a profound importance. The most profound accomplishment would be to create an ongoing, self-sustaining volunteering organization or pipeline for high school students. Unfortunately, many high schools have instituted "service learning" requirements, which sound nice on paper but end up being a little value.

Question: Is California as bad as the right wing says it is?
Answer: Many of the problems that some of the political right point out in California are accurate. State income taxes are high on high income earners, and the California state bureaucracy is monstrous in size and monstrously inefficient. San Francisco really does have a problem with homeless people, including many drug addicts; it's not hard to find needles and human feces on sidewalks. Until a recent crackdown, there was a serious problem with car break-ins; even so, I don't leave anything visible in my car when I park in SF, not even my school parking permit that hangs from my rearview mirror. In San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Jose, and San Diego, petty crime isn't being policed particularly heavily, which is forcing some businesses to take measures. As an example, stores in Westgate Mall in San Jose have their gates to the mall common area closed (if they have outside entrances) and close the changing rooms in the evening. A number of stores have closed, especially in SF and Oakland. The California state legislature has a heavy hand in education, even dictating rules about general education requirements at all California public colleges and universities. And yes, there's a pretty significant DEI component to that, a fact that most folks on the right don't like. They have also made laws that make it more difficult to enact discipline in K-12 schools. At the same time, many of the claims are wrong or overstated. As I noted above, taxes are high on high income earners, but for most of us, the taxes aren't really all that bad. because of regressive taxation and nickel and diming, I paid a higher percentage of my income when I lived in St. Louis WHEN YOU COUNT ALL STATE AND LOCAL TAXES. And taxes certainly are not what makes California expensive (that's housing). Housing costs can easily be double or triple the costs in comparable municipalities elsewhere in the US (e.g., comparing SF to Chicago or St. Louis). Housing is expensive because too many people want to live here, and because both practical and political considerations make it difficult to build new housing. That problem is not going to get solved anytime soon. For as much as I find the state legislators control over general education and other requirements to be frustrating, the motive is to make transfer success a more common outcome. Problems with homeless populations have more to do with weather than anything else; Houston and Dallas would be inundated with homeless people if the temperatures never gone very high or low. The same drug problems in California (heroin, fentanyl, and meth) are equally prevalent elsewhere. California is definitely not a utopia, but it's also not a wasteland. I found that a lot of right wing characterizations have presented California as though it were some scenario out of Mad Max. It's not. As a final note, every year for the last few years there has been some kind of weather-related crisis in Texas that has been poorly handled by both the utilities grids and state response. Houston's problems are exacerbated by… well, I would say poor city planning, but that would imply that there was planning involved. Houston is particularly proud of the fact that, for the purposes of municipal planning, they are a libertarian utopia. Every state and every municipality has its problems. ETA It occurred to me that there is one major issue in California, possibly the worst issue for the long term, and the right never seems to mention it. Our water system is… not good. This is mostly in the southern part of the state, including the Inland Empire. We have enough water for home use, although we have to pipe it around. The big issue is agriculture, where we’re using groundwater far faster than it can be replaced. There is a forthcoming crisis. But the right doesn’t seem worried…

Question: Why is the re-entry point of the Earth's atmosphere so hot from the space that space crafts need heat shields to survive burning?
Answer: I will offer a slightly different take on answering this question. The shortest version is this: it has to happen. The spacecraft starts at rest (relative to the earth) and ends the same way. How did that spacecraft get into space in the first place? Well, it was launched on a rocket, right? And what that rocket did was use a lot of controlled combustion (burning fuel) to impart a lot of energy onto that spacecraft, putting it in motion, accelerating it away from the Earth. In order to get the spacecraft back to rest with respect to the Earth, all of that energy has to go somewhere. If there was no atmosphere, we could just let it plummet right into the ground. There wouldn't be any heat until it hit the ground, but the outcome would not be very good for the spacecraft and whatever it contained. I also wouldn't want to be standing on the ground, because the Earth would absorb most of that energy. Of course the Earth is pretty big and will be fine, but anything standing nearby will not. If the spacecraft had rocket engines and remaining fuel, it could point that rocket in the direction of travel and accelerate in the opposite direction of travel. This is what the Apollo Lunar Module did on the Moon. It's also what SpaceX Rockets do, but they aren't coming from space; these are just the lower stages… for now. The upcoming Starship upper stage will be able to land this way, but not on Earth. It would take too much fuel. So we don't have the ability to slow the spacecraft down with engines and we don't want to let it impact the ground (and couldn't make that happen anyway, because of the atmosphere), so the only way to bleed off all of that energy is to turn it into heat. Conveniently, the atmosphere will do that pretty much automatically with something moving so fast. As others indicate, it doesn't matter that it's coming from space; what matters is that it's 25 times the speed of sound. So the next shortest answer is this: the atmosphere is undoing the work that the rocket did at the beginning, allowing the spacecraft to come back to rest with respect to the earth.

Question: Do I have to take Physics in the IB curriculum to major in computer science, software development, and artificial intelligence in top universities in the US like Princeton, Harvard, MIT, CalTech…etc?

When I was applying to colleges and universities, there was a very standard set of curriculum requirements to even be considered for a competitive college or university, including four years of English, three years of history, four years of mathematics, four years of foreign language, and three specific science courses (biology, chemistry, and physics). Question: I’m a senior aiming for nursing, taking AP Chemistry, Honors Pre-Calc, Anatomy, and two honors social studies. Should I drop Honors American Government and economics for regular classes? Will this affect my chances for a competitive nursing program?
Answer: The nursing programs I have seen have pretty much all been two-stage programs. The first stage is a pre-nursing major, during which you complete prerequisites. Toward the end of this process, you apply for admission into the nursing major itself. At that point, all they are looking at is your prior year (for an ADN/ASN) or two years (for a BSN) of coursework and related activities. As a result, pre-nursing programs tend to not be very competitive to enter. For some, admission to the college or university is sufficient. For ASN/ADM programs, anybody who can enroll at the community college can begin the pre-nursing program. I suppose it's possible that I'm wrong and that the college university you want to attend doesn't work this way. You need to find out where you plan to apply and what their expectations are. One thing that surprises me is that you're not taking an English class; you should make sure that you have enough English credits to get admitted. Generally, my point is this: you're thinking in terms of honors and AP being accolades that will be valuable, but that hasn't been my experience. many colleges and universities require that students take the three core natural sciences: biology, chemistry, and physics. If you have not taken physics but you have taken regular chemistry, you should probably take physics, regardless of whether it's AP, honors, or regular. I suspect that to maximize your chances of admission, your schedule should look something like this: pre-calculus, senior English, physics, history, and foreign language. Having the right credits is much more important than having AP or honors. But you can research this yourself look at several colleges and universities nearby. Or if you are planning to pursue an ASN/ADN, don't worry about it too much; you effectively start over when you start college.

Question: How do university presidents get informed about newly made education laws?
Answer: New education loans are pretty rare. Oh, small chefs happen all the time and things like funding priorities, but new fundamental laws? They're pretty rare. Even before being passed, any significant law would be covered extensively in the Chronicle of Higher Education. What does change are federal regulations. In the of the recent Loper Bright, nobody knows what regulations are actually enforceable. There is currently showdown between the US federal government (and specifically the Department of Education (ED), and even more specifically the Office of Civil Rights (OCR)) and a number of states over new regulations including (but not limited to) access to restrooms and teams for trans students. Ss for how presidents learn of them, more generically how institutions learn of them is through what are called "dear colleague" letters, which are guidance on how the ED plans to enforce the laws. Those publications will be read by the relevant administrators. Have you ever wondered what all those administrators do? Some of them spend a lot of time reading documents like this and figuring out how they impact the operation of the university, in order to keep the university in compliance. I'm not kidding when I say that much of the increased expense of our universities is a consequence of the high-level of regulation. In addition, any large college or university will have in-house counsel, and those that don't will have a firm on retainer. These will be lawyers who specialize in education law and regulation. Also, administrators travel to conferences and workshops to learn about these things and talk with their colleagues about how to best implement them. Neither of these is particularly cheap. Over the next few years, you should anticipate a number of court decisions dramatically decreasing the power of the federal government to regulate… well, everything. That includes higher education. Sadly, this is actually going to increase expenses for universities for a while, because everything will be in flux. In addition, some states will create laws pushing institution in one direction or another (much as we are seeing some states demand that institutions increase their DEI activity, while other states are preventing public institutions from having DEI programs at all). But to summarize the answer, university presidents and other administrators have direct access to guidance from OCR, access to higher education publications like the Chronicle of Higher Education, and routine attend meetings on these topics, in addition to getting direct guidance from lawyers who specialize in education.

Question: What are some very difficult degrees that, with dedication and hard work, can be pursued by both average and highly intelligent individuals, regardless of their level of difficulty?
Answer: How can something be very difficult and then be evaluated regardless of its level of difficulty? This is one of the types of questions I get on Quora that genuinely frustrate me; I think you're asking for something straightforward that you've wrapped in language that doesn't really make sense. I think what you're asking for are degree programs in which somebody of average intellect can be successful. So far, so good, but then you throw in the stuff about difficulty and highly intelligent and I'm lost. I'll give you my general response. Intellect will only take you so far. Someone with genuinely modest intellect is going to struggle earning any kind of secondary degree, but a lot of very intelligent people struggle with the same thing. Why? Because you need work habits, time management skills, and learning skills. If you don't have those, intelligence is really just an abstract idea. Another factor: interest. Regardless of intelligence, somebody who isn't sufficiently interested won't be able to have the motivation to do the work. I have had successful students ranging from plodders who get through by hard work and to those who will go on to PhD's and more successful careers than I could ever aspire to. Of course, I've had students who weren't particularly bright and didn't succeed, but I've also had exceptional students who simply couldn't deal with criticism or feedback, lacked the focus to make progress, or had a poor level of self control and couldn't get the work done. They all ended up in the same place. I remember one guy had a degree in computer engineering coming back for a degree in computer science. He freely admitted he had not done much work for his engineering degree and didn't really have any skills; he was stocking shelves at Lowes, and he was tired of it.

Question: The left tells us the rich don't pay taxes, the data says the poor don't, aren't new government programs then paid by the middle class either through taxes or inflation?
Answer: The problem is that you were using the generic word "tax". There are lots of different kinds of taxes. Almost everybody who works pays federal taxes, but they don't necessarily pay federal income taxes. Those only start when you hit a certain level, and if you have children, that level goes up with fair bit, thanks to the Earned Income Tax Credit. Less than half of all taxpayers pay any federal income tax, and almost all of them have low income. However, wealthy people have… well, you can call them tricks, you can call them loopholes, but they're really just advantageous tax laws that allow them to minimize their federal income tax. Wealthy people have accountants and lawyers who help them use these laws to minimize their income, or put their income in the right categories, or avoid realizing the income. The specifics don't really matter here; these tax laws have been written to the advantage of very wealthy people , and that seems unlikely to change. By far the most fundamental shift in taxation in the years since World War II is the move from corporate taxation to worker taxation. At one point, businesses paid about 2/3 of all federal tax revenue, with individuals paying 1/3. Those proportions have now switched. If you think that wealthy individuals have good accountants, lawyers, and lobbyist, you need to look at big corporations. It is true that rich people pay a lot of tax on a per-person basis. However, the Obama administration managed to convince Congress to better fund the IRS. They hired new agents, built new software systems, and took advantage of other new technology and have now brought in billions in back taxes. I can tell you that money didn't come from auditing folks who work at McDonald's. Donald Trump and the GOP tried very hard to decrease IRS funding for enforcement, but the Republicans didn't control both houses of Congress. Let's be clear: this is not about raising taxes. None of this was about removing the advantageous tax laws. This is just about making sure that people actually pay the taxes they owe. Some people object to that. I don't; I pay my share. I don't like it, and anybody who says "I love paying taxes because good things happen…", well, they aren't wrong, but I don't love to pay taxes. I'd love for those things to happen without me paying taxes. But I accept that I have to pay taxes, and I do. I get pissed off when other people decide that the rules (which again have been written to their advantage in the first place) don't apply to them.
