Question: Why do yanks call universities “college” when college in USA only refers to community colleges and junior colleges and not tertiary institutions named “universities”?
Answer: I’m not really sure what I can add to Ben and Kim‘s answer, but I have some thoughts. With one exception, the use of the term “college“ in the UK and the US aren’t dramatically different. The exception is using “college“ to refer to where an undergraduate studies, rather than “university“ (as in “I went to college”). In the UK, college can refer to a sixth form college, a non-degree granting postsecondary institution, a standalone degree-granting postsecondary institution (the Royal College of Art), an organizational or residential unit with in a university (All Souls College), or a professional organization (Royal College of Surgeons). In the United States, “college“ can refer to a number of different types of degree granting institutions, but it can also refer to an organizational unit within a university. In addition, several large universities have retained the word “college“ as their title (Dartmouth College and Boston College are well-known examples). What’s the commonality? The term “college“ is a convenient term for several different kinds of educational institutions. As for why we use the term “college” more in the US, that’s historical. When the first colleges were opened in the United States, they were modeled after colleges in the UK. The only extant universities in England at the time were Oxford and Cambridge. It would have seemed absurd to name the first American institutions as “universities”; they were small organizations. As a result, the term for a post secondary institution in the US became “college”, rather than university. British people rarely seem to grasp the scale often seem to fail to grasp the scale of the United States. The first two colleges in the United States were Harvard College (founded in New Towne, Massachusetts) and the College of William and Mary (founded in Williamburg, Virginia). By modern roads, Cambridge (New Towne changed its name) and Williamsburg are about 950 km apart. Compare that to Oxford and Cambridge, only 130 km apart. Large distances between population centers caused academic institutions to remain small for a very long period of time, and we had many more. Nine colleges were founded and chartered while America was still a colony. All are now universities, granting a large number and significant variety of postgraduate degrees but two (Dartmouth College and the College of William and Mary) have retained the word “college“ in their titles. So, yeah, history. Also, Americans use the word school to refer to… well, any type of school. Any academic institution, which is what the word means. It can refer to anything from an kindergarten to a university. We even refer to all postgraduate study as “grad school“. If that bothers you, OK. When an American asks you “Where did you go to school?“, they may or may not be asking you about where you earned your undergraduate degree; you will have to figure that out from context.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Why is coach Walz proud that none of his students could ever get into good colleges like Vance's Yale?
Answer: I think you’ve misunderstood the point that Walz was trying to make. Vance actually went to college at Ohio State and then earned his JD from Yale. Walz attended Chadron State College and earned his MS from Mankato State University. Any reasonably objective person will conclude that JD Vance has a more impressive academic background. But note that they’re both vying for the same job. Vance might get it or Walz might get it, but where they earned their degrees seems to be a little consequence. I have known people who earned undergraduate and graduate degrees at pretty much every impressive college and university in the US. I’ve also known people who earned their degrees at places I’ve never heard of, some of whom started at community colleges. If you can attend Yale or Ohio State and you feel like they are good fits, go ahead and do so. If your best choices are Chadron State College or Mankato State University, go and don’t worry about it. FDR went to Harvard, but Harry Truman barely attended college and certainly never graduated. Eisenhower went to West Point. Kennedy went to Harvard, but LBJ went Southwest State Teachers College. Nixon went Whittier College, Ford went to Michigan (and then Yale), Carter to the US Naval Academy, and Reagan to Eureka College. Do you see the pattern? Because I don’t see one at all. Perhaps if I had gone to Yale…

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What type of science is a "solid" program to study in university? I'm interested in food nutrition and biology, and am thinking of options such as working for a large company after graduating. Could there also be other job ideas?
Answer: Not only solids, but all states of matter are primarily covered in physics, although they are relevant in chemistry, too. Of course, you need mathematics to help describe the shape of the solids, along with calculating things like surface area and volume. As for thinking about working for a large company, you haven’t put the cart before the horse; you put the cart on the track when you don’t even have a horse. Don’t worry about things like that until you have started searching for your second or third professional job. You do need to get involved in career prep, but you don’t necessarily need to decide your major today. I have no idea food science actually leads to good jobs; it may or it may not. Again, career prep will help you find that information out.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do you feel one-to-one initiatives (laptops, iPads, Chromebooks) have impacted student learning in high school? Is this a practice that should continue?
Answer: Eh. For some students, access to a computer can benefit their education, but for other students they are just magic distraction machines. And it doesn’t matter if they should continue; they will. There’s just too much inertia And too much technology has been built into the educational process to move away from one: one. However, I admire teachers who say, “now it’s time to put away your computers and take out your notebooks”.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do I get extra credits in a US high school if I am arriving from overseas for 11th grade?
Answer: That largely depends on what you mean by “get extra credits“. If you are moving to the US and are worried that you will not be able to graduate high school two years, I would encourage you to not worry. If you have been studying appropriate topics, you will be given credit for the work you’ve done. If you find that you don’t have all of the courses you need to graduate on time, you will be able to take some of them in the summer between your junior and senior years. Nobody gets any benefit from keeping a well educated student in high school for a longer period of time.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is there any technical/HND course for students after O levels like some diploma in furniture design or vehicle maintenance and is it available for international students in UK and in which colleges?
Answer: These things sound like subjects that would be covered by BTEC, not at a university. I don’t know about the UK, but many countries do not admit international students for trade programs, including the US (with limited exceptions).

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I've traveled the world and won over 100,000 thousand dollars playing Fortnite. How good of an extracurricular is that for the top 30?
Answer: I didn’t know it was possible to win $100 million playing Fortnite. As for “the top 30“, you need to list out what you think the top 30 are, because there’s no consensus. Even then, I think the general answer is that, based on what you’ve told us, you aren’t a particularly competitive candidate on the basis of these extra credit activities. OK, you’re a very good Fortnite player. Wonderful. What does that mean? And as for traveling the world, that’s a function of wealth, And most of these institutions that you imagine to be so important have plenty of wealthy applicants. Getting back to your question, you wrote 100,000 thousand, which is 100 million. I inferred that this would be in dollars. These kinds of casual mistakes are easy to make, but they are also the kind of thing that quickly gets an application dismissed. Yes, I know, you’re going to put more effort into your application materials than into a Quora question, but that’s beside the point. If you want to be a better writer, you want people to point out these kinds of mistakes for you.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Do I meet the requirements to become a speech language pathology assistant in Florida?
Answer: Reviewing the ChatGPT transcript, I actually think ChatGPT is correct here; these courses may fit, but they may not. While I commend you for a good use of ChatGPT, I think you’re going to have to contact the organization that provides the certification. They will have fairly well developed rubrics and should be able to quickly answer your question, but these rubrics generally aren’t public.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What are the extracurricular activities that Harvard, Stanford, Princeton, and Yale applicants list on their applications?
Answer: Applicants to the schools will mention every activity under the sun. Admitted students tend to not have laundry lists of extracurricular activities; these schools have been very explicit in encouraging students to have impact in something that is important to them, rather than to sign up. To put it another way, they don’t care if you were a participant in a club or the club president; they want to know what you did while you were participating.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do you write a research statement for a master’s program, when you have only done a research project in a bachelor's and haven't done any SPSS?
Answer: SPSS is a statistical analysis tool. It will not help you write a research statement. The way you learn to write research statements is to read research papers and then try to write your own ideas out and get feedback on them. There are a few basic parts: what is your research problem, why is it important to you, what methods would you use to better understand the problem, and what is your rough plan for analyzing any results.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is it possible to survive with a PhD stipend in Canada?
Answer: Canada is a big country with absurdly expensive big cities, expensive moderate sized cities, more affordable moderate sized cities, and reasonably affordable small cities. There may be some other variants in there, too. However, Canada produces a significant number of PhD each year, so the basic answer is “yes”. A more specific answer depends on the city where you will be living in, the stipend amount itself, and your needs. A single person who doesn’t mind having roommates is in a radically different financial position than a married person supporting a spouse and children.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I can’t decide if I should go to the Air Force or college. What are the pros and cons of both and some advice?
Answer: You really have six possibilities: I think the major deciding factor is whether you want to be enlisted or a commissioned officer. I’ve known people who have served as one or the other or (in some cases) as both. Everything i have observed has confirmed that they are very different experiences. My impression (as somebody who has worked as a civilian for research facilities that are part of the Air Force and Navy, but never served) Is that the Air Force is the most technical of the services, with a strong emphasis on knowledge and skills related to technology. More knowledge and skills are beneficial. But I think your first decision is whether you want to serve listed or as an officer. There are many online resources that discuss the two experiences side-by-side. Oh, if you want to be a pilot in the Air Force, you must be an officer.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Should I try for Ph.D (in bioinformatics) in the US/other countries if I already have an offer from Tsinghua University?
Answer: The only reason I know of that would recommend you pursuing a PhD in the US would be if you want/expect to work in the US after finishing your PhD. Education is local, and it’s harder (not impossible, but difficult) to come to the US for a career if you earned your PhD outside of the US. I can’t tell you whether or not to accept the offer from Tsinghua University. That will depend on the expectations of where you hope to land after completing your PhD.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is my dissertation, in the form of a forum discussion, ready to be rewritten as a journal paper or perhaps even two or more papers?
Answer: This is a question for your dissertation advisor. If you do not have a dissertation advisor, the answer is “no, get a dissertation advisor.” In the US, we do not award PhDs by publication. The only way to get a PhD is to enter a PhD program and complete all of the required coursework and examinations and then complete a dissertation. If you were able to write a complete dissertation on your own, all of the work for the program should be trivial.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: My Gen Z friend says what's the point of working if your salary barely covers your living expenses. What should I tell her?
Answer: The economy sucks for young people. There are relatively few entry-level jobs, housing is expensive, and recent inflation has undermined real income. But… there are jobs. If your salary covers your living expenses when you first get a job, that’s a huge win. Perhaps your friend has the option of moving home with her parents. If so, great, wonderful for her. But where does that lead? Someone can gripe all they want about the problems of capitalism or that prior generations had it easier, but in the end, that accomplishes absolutely nothing. If someone wants their life to be better, they have only one choice, which is to move aggressively forward. Your friend is welcome to stay with her parents, but then she shouldn’t expect her life to change.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can I get an admission to a college or university in the USA with a CGPA of 2.8 as an international student to pursue an undergraduate degree?
Answer: If you have completed your secondary education (equivalent to high school) in your home country, there is a college or university in the United States that will admit you. In fact, there are quite a number that will admit you. The problem is paying for it; plan minimum cost of $30,000 a year including tuition, fees, and board, mandatory health insurance, personal expenses, and travel. If you want to attend a university you heard of or one that is not located in a rural area, far from any city, the costs go up rapidly and at some institutions climb to $100,000 a year. You will need to have that $30,000 or whatever for your first year in the bank before you will be given a visa.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I have finished 11 years of school in my country and I would like to study in some Australian universities. Should I apply directly to a becholar or to a diploma (foundation year)?
Answer: Assuming you can gain admission (in the United States, college/university students are expected to have completed 12 years of school) and have the financial means, why would you not choose a foundation year? It will allow you to strengthen your skills in addition to your academic subjects, and will let you acclimate to Australian higher education. I don't know what the costs are or how wealthy you are; earning a degree in a foreign country is an expensive endeavor and not for people who don't have a high degree of wealth using an international scale (excluding students who are truly among the best in their nation, who can often receive scholarships).

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is medical school boring? Will I regret it?
Answer: If you are like my friends who went to medical school, you will find it boring and regret your decision. You will also find it fascinating and have absolute confidence in your decision. Any challenging post graduate program is going to be something of an emotional roller coaster, with plenty of parts that are frustrating. If you aren't prepared for some bad mixed in with the good, then I wouldn't go, but if you think that the rewards will outweigh the downsides, then I wouldn't worry about it too much.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What are my chances in medical school with all 6s in GCSE and about to to A levels in Chemistry, Maths, and psychology?
Answer: To get into medical school in the UK, you need high A level grades. Given your GCSE results, I don't see that outcome happening unless you simply did no consistent studying and have a concrete plan to improve (not an intention, a plan) for your A levels. In the UK system, it generally makes more sense to focus on your strengths, and I suspect if you were on your GSE results, you know which subjects were easier for you. Psychology shouldn't be much of an issue, but if you do not have a natural affinity for science and mathematics I would recommend making other plans. As another answer notes, there are medical pathways in BTEC, too.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What do I truly need to learn and do to become a successful software engineer?
Answer: Being a software engineer is a lot like being a professional writer; in fact, it really is just a particular form of professional writing. Any professional writer worth their salt will tell you the same thing: the way to become a good writer is to start as a bad writer and then write. You will write a lot of bad… whatever, poems, stories, code. If there’s one distinct advantage to pursuing a degree in computer science, it’s that you will write a lot of bad code and get feedback on how to make it better. This is one reason why undergraduate degrees in software engineering don’t make sense; a masters degree does, because by the time you pursue a master’s degree, you have already written a lot of bad code. If you have industry experience (which you should before entering a software engineering graduate program), you’ve also seen a lot of bad code, and seen how real-world projects progress over time. Once you have written enough bad code (you will never stop writing bad code, but the balance will hopefully be more toward good code), you can start thinking about how to be an successful software engineer. Software engineering is a weird combination of skills that include but extend far beyond programming. You won’t get very far in soft engineering if you don’t have communication skills, software design skills, troubleshooting skills, learning skills, and social skills. Figure out which of those you are weakest in and work on it. Beyond that, you need to decide what “successful“ means for you personally. Perhaps you just want to maintain employment and feel that you’re staying somewhat current with technology. Perhaps you want to make a lot of money, work for a famous company, and/or regularly progress up a career ladder. But start by writing bad code. Then figure out how to make it better.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What’s the best path for me to become a GC? Currently in first semester, going for my MBA. Should I stay or go to a trade school? I want to become a GC and eventually have my own GC firm.
Answer: I suspect you were referring to being a general contractor. Doesn’t quite make sense, but it’s the only thing that would relate to trade school. If you are referring to being general counsel, Beheruz is correct about going to law school, and he’s definitely correct that we can’t read your mind and GC Could stand for any number of things. To be a general contractor in most of the US, you need a contractor license. Not all general contractors come up through the building trades, but it’s by far the most common way to get there. That probably but doesn’t necessarily mean going to trade school; in some building trades, apprenticeship doesn’t involve a formal school. You’re going to need to look into your options for that. In the past, it was nearly impossible to get into most of the building trades if you didn’t have a connection, typically your father, grandfather, or uncle. That’s less the case now. All general contractors need clients. One reason to go through a trade program is to develop a reputation and connections. Would an MBA helped somebody who was a general contractor, presumably one large enough to have a firm and multiple employees and subcontractors? Sure. Why not. But that’s not how you get there; you get there by basic qualifications, building and network, and eventually soliciting clients. I have to admit that I’m a bit disappointed in this question. Somebody who is prepared to pursue an MBA should be sophisticated enough to find some general contractors in the area, look them up on LinkedIn, and see what their backgrounds were. I would recommend that as your next step after reading this answer. if you didn’t intend to ask about general contracting or being general counsel, then please clarify.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I appreciate Aussies will protect their own, but how can anyone defend Rachael Gunn's performance at the Paris Olympics? She was atrocious.
Answer: In recent decades, we’ve seen an increase in people who essentially gamed the system to get into the Olympics. Elizabeth Swaney, a (very) amateur American athlete, attended as many relevant competitions as possible to earn enough points to qualify for the women’s halfpipe event at the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics. She succeeded by performing unchallenging runs with no errors. She qualified to ski for Hungary because her grandparents were Hungarian; she had previously tried the same thing with the skeleton and Venezuala, but failed to qualify. Per Wikipedia, “Thirteen of her top 30 finishes were a result of her showing up, not falling, and recording a score.” At the Olympics, she performed few stunts and earned scores of 30.00 and 31.40, placing her last, still significantly below the next-lowest competitor, who fell on both of her runs. Swaney was framed as having manipulated the system and having been mercenary, competing for a country with which she had little relationship.[1] A few years ago at the World University Games, a runner from Somalia produced an embarrassing result; it turned out that she didn’t legitimately qualify and was the niece of the chairwoman of the Somali Athletics Federation. The runner, Nasra Ali Abukar, ran the 100m in 21.81 seconds. If sustained, that would be a 3:41 kilometer. At my fastest, I’ve run a 5km race at a sub-5-minute pace. Admittedly slower, but for 50 times longer. I don’t know if I could run a 21.81 100m, but I wouldn't be much behind, and I’m not a competitive athlete and a fair bit older. Her aunt, Khadijo Aden Dahir, was forced to resign. Ali Abukar later claimed to have run with a sprained ankle, but an investigation showed that she had no history of running and she admitted to having only one month of training.[2] All of this is separate from the rare, entertaining examples of hardworking athletes from countries that might not have athletes in a particular sport. Eddie the Eagle, Michael Edwards of the UK, had been a committed (if unexceptional) skier before moving to the ski jump and took it quite seriously.[3] Similarly, Eric the Eel, Eric Moussambani of Equitorial Guinea, was a serious swimmer who had little access to swimming facilities and no access to coaching.[4] Both placed last, and Moussambani had the slowest 100m freestyle recorded in Olympic history (by far), but I think what resonated about both men is that they were earnest underdogs. So now to Rachel Gunn, aka raygun. Her performance in breakdancing at the Paris Olympics was the stuff of legend (and not in a good way); NBC/Peacock has apparently removed all actual breakdancing competition footage (not just raygun’s) from the Olympics Portal.[5] OK, so far it’s just a poor performance. There are some problems. There were accusations that she manipulated the Australian Olympic Team selection process and that her husband was a judge, but both of those claims were demonstrated to be false, despite being repeated across the internet.[6] The Australian Olympic Committee succeeded in getting a change dot org petition removed on the basis of containing falsehoods. But… there are still a few issues. First, while she won the championship that gave her the Olympic berth… well, watch the video yourself.[7] You can see the women’s semifinals starting at 1:20. A brief warning: the MC is probably the most annoying person in existence, but admittedly this crowd seemingly did not want to be hyped. Anyway, even considering that none of the dancing would have been competitive in Paris and there is an official scoring system, I don’t see how Raygun won. Second, her casual performance while hanging out with the rest of the Australian Olympic Team[8] seemed much better than her competition performance, but I am struggling to find any long clip of her actual competition. I’ll link a video with some outtakes.[9] NBC has apparently aggressively issued takedown notices whenever those clips appear, despite not doing so for countless other Olympics clips. Third, she’s an academic who studies breakdancing. She has written and spoken about “decolonizing” breakdancing. I’m not sure that anyone knows what that means, but it forces us to ask a question of whether or not she’s hypocritical for objecting to “cultural appropriation” while competing. I don’t have answers to any of these concerns. I don’t care much, other than satisfying my own curiosity. In my final analysis, there seems to be something concerning, but compared to outright cheating and doping, it’s not important or terrible. I think the third point is what really gave the story its momentum.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can I lie to a university about already holding an offer with them to get an offer?
Answer: It's conceptually possible, but that really couldn't play out for undergraduate admission in the United States, and it would likely backfire for most graduate admissions. In addition, universities can throw you out or even rescind your degree if they found out you lied and/or cheated. And yes, it has happened. A fairly famous case at Harvard ended with the student in serious legal trouble, in addition to being thrown out and having all completed academic work rescinded.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can I put my undergraduate research thesis (100pgs, not published) as a writing sample when applying for graduate schools?
Answer: Generally speaking, graduate programs that ask for writing sample will specify what they are looking for. They won't give you a word or page count, but they typically don't want something that's 100 pages long. Certainly nobody will read 100 pages. Look through the work you've done and find something that you feel proud of, both in the work (that the writing demonstrates) you did and how well you think you've explained the work. Realistically, it should probably be a chapter of your research thesis, but for some reason many undergraduate seem to not break their theses into chapters.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do you avoid overspending during the back-to-school season?
Answer: Any question like this has the same generic answer: make a budget and stick to it. You need to start by figuring out how much money you have (including paychecks that may not have come yet), what your ongoing income will be, what your mandatory expenses are going to be, and then the expenses for things you want and/or need. When you get past the absolute mandatory expenses (e.g., rent, tuition, etc.), you need to prioritize everything. Sometimes priorities can be broken down in unusual ways. For example, you might allocate (I'm just making up numbers) $80 for groceries to buy a giant bag of rice, some eggs eggs, an onion, soy sauce, and cooking oil. Do I recommend that you live off of fried rice? No. Further down on the priority list you might allocate additional money for buying additional protein and produce, but you at least have basic food to eat. I often see young people make legitimate complaints about a challenging economy that they had no hand in creating, and then turn around and spend large amounts of money frivolously. Just because the economy sucks and inflation has been high doesn't mean you shouldn't control your budget; in fact, it just makes that budget control that much more valuable. We often spend a surprising amount of money on what was referred to as "zooming" in a paper I read many years ago. This is when we spend money on things we don't need or we choose a more expensive option. Consider coffee; zooming would be buying a Keurig and pods or buying drinks at Starbucks. Supermarket prices for bulk coffee, milk, and sugar (if you insist on adding those in) are much, much lower then Keurig pods, and lower still than an occasional Starbucks (one every few days). That doesn't mean you shouldn't set aside money for some unnecessary/fun spending, but you really want to both limit it and make it highly visible. Looking back on how I lived in college and the first couple of years of my professional life, I'm stunned at how efficient I could be with money. Buying food on sale takes time and a bit of effort, but it's much easier now with the Internet; we used to have to get the Sunday paper and cut coupons out of the coupon section. Even if your course syllabi aren't published yet, your university bookstore should know what books you are required to buy. You can incorporate those into your budget right now. If they are expensive (and many are), it's perfectly reasonable to email the professor and ask if an older edition is an acceptable substitute (any professor who requires students to purchase a $150 book (let alone $300) should be prepared for this question). I've moved a fair bit in my adult life, often long distances. I once had a student, a Navy officer, who reflected that every move involved about $1000 in somewhat hidden and largely unavoidable expenses, and he wasn't wrong. Things like cleaning supplies a great example of items that can quickly add up. Some planning can dramatically cut or eliminate costs. Ask relatives or family friends if they have some half used cleaning supplies sitting around in the back of a cabinet; pretty much everybody has something. Garage sales, yard sales, thrift stores like Goodwill or St. Vincent de Paul, and discount and dollar stores are all great places to find bargains. Many waste disposal facilities (dumps) have stores where they sell items from bulk pick up or that were dropped off (no, they don't go through trash); I got some great deals at the Marina dump when I moved into my current apartment, including a nice lamp. Another planning-related issue is time management. Good time management means that you have more time to do things like cook food at home or pack a lunch. As with most kinds of changes, becoming more budget-minded isn't something you complete overnight. Start by identifying some areas where you can cut back spending and focus on those. The very first thing you should do, though, is developed at least a rough budget. A few final notes:

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I've been told choosing languages as a major is a waste of my hard work and intelligence, and that it won't provide good salary. How much can I make learning languages fluently and how? (One of the foreign languages being English)
Answer: This is one of the challenges with how people understand education versus how it impacts employment. Generally speaking, you can't make any money from learning other languages; you must be able to use your knowledge of that language in a job to earn money. The most obvious jobs are translation and interpretation, but there really aren't that many jobs in those fields in that world. Much of the casual translation work is now handled by automated tools, which aren't great when there's anything serious at stake, but are fine for many casual purposes (e.g., describing the amenities at a hotel). To become an interpreter, you must not only have strong fluency and at least two languages, you typically have to complete an academic program. But there are many careers in which speaking more than one language provides a huge advantage. Most software development jobs don't benefit hugely from multiple language fluency, but if you have those skills, you can do specialized work. There are definitely other rules in software development and information technology where multiple language fluency can be beneficial. Even more mundane careers can benefit; I recall a bartender at a hotel in Manhattan was able to make a fair bit of money in a low stress environment because she spoke multiple languages and worked at a hotel that catered to European travelers. The list of jobs where multiple language fluency can be useful is quite long. As with everyone else considering higher education, I encourage you to start exploring careers that might interest you and find educational programs that will help you get there. The US Department of Labor offers a free tool for career investigation called My Next Move. Complete the interest inventory and look at Zones 4 & 5.[1]

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Will there ever be a pill that can replace food?
Answer: Weeeeeeeell… sort of. Yes. It's been done. But not permanently. Of course, answers from Vivian and others are correct. You can't completely replace food with a pill. Eventually, you need nutrients in larger bulk than you could swallow. But for a period of time, you can use drugs to keep people going. It's incredibly dangerous, but it has been done. It's fairly commonly known that the Nazis used methamphetamine to keep the Wehrmacht marching and the Luftwaffe flying, but a more interesting drug was D-IX, which combined methamphetamine with cocaine and oxycodone. It was never produced or distributed in large quantities because of resource limitations, but the Nazis did test it on prisoners at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp.[1] The Allies didn't use methamphetamine, they used Benzedrine, a trademark for amphetamine. I highly recommend the Secrets of the Dead episode "World War Speed", which covers WWII stimulant use.[2] But you can also just use supplements if the person already has the calories. One of the more amazing and bizarre stories in the annals of medical history is that of Angus Barbieri's 382-day fast. This was never the recommended approach, but after a short supervised fast in the hospital, Barbieri continued fasting mostly at home (but with regular checkups) for over a year, losing 275 lbs. (125 kg). He consumed only supplements, mild stimulants (coffee and tea), water, and yeast for amino acids. DO NOT TRY ANY OF THIS AT HOME. Or really don't try it at all.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can I do a postdoc or get a teaching position in a top university after graduating from TAMU?
Answer: Maybe? The issue is not that you earned your PhD from Texas A&M. The criteria for hiring faculty and postdocs rarely rests primarily on the institution; the focus is on whether a candidate has a high level of the necessary skills and a track record of growth. There are far more positions in some fields than others. If you have a PhD in the humanities, you should set your aspirations very low. There are far too many humanities PhDs being produced, and while not yet dying, the humanities are most common areas for cutting whole programs and faculty lines because students have little interest in those fields anymore (from a numerical standpoint). In most of STEM, there are plenty of postdocs. The NSF and the NIH fund research across STEM, and a very high proportion of money funds postdoctoral scholars. They’re inexpensive compared to faculty, and they’re more productive than PhD students. However, permanent faculty positions are harder to come by, especially in the natural sciences. I am astounded by the research productivity of my peers in our natural science departments. They publish extensively, bring in big grants, develop programs for students, and are involved in outreach. Over in CS, we’re just keeping our heads above water by comparison. Most of them spent years in postdocs at prestigious institutions, while most of us in CS went directly into faculty positions. And as for teaching positions, some people think, “well, I’m not good enough at research, so I will go into teaching.” I can’t say that never works, but universities have been expanding their full-time teaching faculty roles. Most of the people who have teaching roles (at least, of those I’ve met) made a conscious decision to commit themselves to teaching and are very, very good at it. Many also conduct research into field-specific education (e.g., mathematics education), too. Some even bring in large grants and supervise PhD students.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Which tech company does everyone think is #1 in California?

Question: I’m a US citizen and a natural born in the Philippines. I plan to study for college in the Philippines and major in medical, nursing or in becoming a radiologist. Should I do it or just do community college in US?
Answer: The problem is cost. I assume that you currently reside in the Philippines. If you and your parents live in the Philippines, neither of your parents is active duty military, you probably can't claim residency in any state. That means that you must either pay out of state tuition or attend a private college or university. it is possible to establish residency in the US and it's generally a bit easier if your parents don't live here but that usually requires living here for at least a year. That can be the best choice, but for nursing and the Philippines specifically, I am skeptical. As you may know, the Philippines is a source for many nurses who come to the US. One of the advantages of that pathway is an ability to get a visa, which you don't need, but the pathway does prepare you for licensure as a nurse in the US. A rough low end cost estimate for annual expenses as an out-of-state student pursuing a bachelor's degree in the US is about $30,000 And you study for four years (so $120,000 total). If you are pursuing an associate's degree in nursing, it only shortens by one year, and for out-of-state students, community colleges aren't that much cheaper; let's estimate a total cost of $75,000, and you don't have a bachelors degree at the end of that, although (assuming you pass) are an RN. It's also possible to study for one or two years and find that, even if you have earned strong grades, you aren't competitive enough for admission into the nursing program itself. You would be eligible for federal financial aid (including a Pell grant) and may get some institutional aid, and I don't know the total cost of earning a bachelor's degree in nursing in the Philippines, but I have to imagine that (even considering aid you might get), the cost of your education in the Philippines will be a fraction of what it would be in the US. Higher education in the United States is more expensive than just about anywhere else. If you want to pursue an MD and become a physician, things get more complicated, and you would probably be better off earning your bachelor's degree in the US. However, as competitive as nursing programs are, medical school is even more competitive. A rough estimate of the number of people who start college in the US intending to go to medical school and actually complete medical school within the next decade is 10%. my general recommendations:

Question: Can a person with color blindness get into a college like Harvard or MIT in the field of physics?
Answer: Given the prevalence of colorblindness, about one in every twelve men, dozens are admitted to MIT, at least some of whom will major in physics. Question: Is there an opportunity for international students to take a credit transfer program to upgrade their degree from an associate degree to a bachelor’s degree? Is there a scholarship for that program?
Answer: If you have an associate’s degree or equivalent, you can apply as a transfer student to most colleges and universities in the US (both award bachelor’s degrees). Which courses will transfer? The only way to know is to contact each individual institution. I know that some institutions in the US have articulation programs with institutions in other countries (we have one with a college in India), but I assume you are not on such a program. Before you bother pursuing this, realize that a good estimate of the lowest possible cost to study in the US is about $30,000 a year. That’s not before financial aid or scholarships; that’s the minimum (unless you are one of the best students in your country, but if you were, you would know it). If you do not have that much money and cannot get it, then this would simply be an exercise in frustration.

Question: If I've done 4 years of graduation from Pakistan, Can I study Bachelor's again in the US or a European Country? The main reason is that IELTS requirements are higher for master's programs. Also, I want to change my field of study, is it possible?
Answer: Absolutely, if you can afford the $30,000 or more a year it will cost to pursue a bachelor’s degree in the US. And that’s not for an institution you have ever heard of or located in a place that will interest you. That’s an approximate baseline of the lowest cost you will find. Most institutions will be more expensive. There are not scholarships or aid for students pursuing a second degree (and they’re quite rare for students pursuing a first degree).

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I was expelled from Birmingham City University due to a delayed fee installment. They informed the Home Office, and now my visa will be canceled within 60 days. This has severely impacted my life. What can I do?
Answer: Fair or not, reasonable or not, you have not met the terms of your visa, which invariably include meeting financial obligations. In the US, it would be unusual for a university to act on a single delayed payment, especially if the student contacted the university to explain the situation and when they planned to rectify the issue. Perhaps that’s not the case in the UK, but I suspect that you either did not contact the university or do not have a plan to cover that payment. Since you have not met the terms of your visa, it has been canceled. If you can pay the fees, contact the university ASAP. It may be possible to stop the cancellation. However, if you cannot pay the fee, I don’t see a resolution. You will need to leave the UK.

Question: How does being accepted into a prestigious university, achieving excellence in academics, winning a sports championship, etc. exploit the so called "successful" and "winners" by breeding pride in the capitalist society?
Answer: OK, that question took a left turn. It doesn't quite make sense, but I think I can tease some bits out. First, I think you're talking about the problems of meritocracy; we celebrate achievement, but achievement is often tied to opportunity and ability. I probably live a more comfortable life than somebody who doesn't have the same natural affinity for computer science and/or didn't have access to the kind of education I received. In other words, pure chance has given me things that other people won't be able to get. I don't completely accept that model; I had to work hard to get where I am, and I'm expected to (and do) contribute back to society. But I get it; why them and not me? I don't think I can persuade you to my perspective, but compared to prior societies on earth, at least I'm not being celebrated because a few generations ago my great, great grandfather was really good at lopping off the heads of his enemies. Now, as for "breeding pride in the capitalist society", I'm pretty damn proud of what capitalism has accomplished. It doesn't really make sense; if you looked at the two systems abstractly, you might easily conclude that communism would produce more opportunity and material comfort for the average person than capitalism, but the opposite is true. Life in communist society is stultifying and dangerous, and they have never achieved anything close to "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs." I would say we've done more to accomplish that under capitalism. I will go further and argue that what we think we understand about capitalism isn't accurate. I often refer people to Deirdre McCluskey's "Bourgeois Trilogy", in which she explains that the success of capitalism isn't due to the accumulation of capital, but the creation of a whole class of knowledge workers.

Question: What do you think of Leah Remini's exposure work against the Church of Scientology? Do you agree with what's she doing? Why?
Answer: I think there are better (in the sense of more informative) exposes, in particular Jenna Miscavige Hill's book Beyond Belief and Ron Miscavige's book Ruthless. Jenna and Ron are (respectively) the niece and father of David Miscavige, the leader of Scientology since shortly after L Ron Hubbard's death in the mid 80s. However, relatively few stars have left Scientology, especially from the group of true believers. Remini is not a major Hollywood figure, but she's a household name, and her expose may well have had more impact than the books above combined because she wrote it. Regardless, she has no reason to lie and published the book at significant personal cost and risk. I don't think that her book is what stood between her and higher levels of fame, but her life would have been much simpler had she remained distantly affiliated with Scientology or just wandered away and kept her mouth shut. I think it says a lot about a person courage and values in general when they take risks and face consequences in order to help other people, and I think that was a prime motivator for her. I admire her As for whether or not I agree with what she's doing, she's facing down one of the most nefarious legal organizations in the United States. The amount of abuse perpetrated in the name of Scientology is unreal. That is above and beyond the nonsensical "woo" that they sell to people just looking to get a better handle on their lives, often spending far more than they can afford. Scientology is sometimes likened to or even considered a religion. I have a lot of respect for religions, and I don't belittle anyone's religious belief. If I had a friend or family member who was exploring just about any religion I've ever heard of, it wouldn't concern me. I have had close friends from just about every major religion on the planet, and friends who are agnostic or atheist. However, if a friend or family member started to express interest in Scientology, I would do my level best to keep them away from it.

Question: I’m a Korean student who wants to go to a U.S. university. Can you tell me how high grade I should get to have a scholarship in good universities in the US (GPA, SAT, AP, etc.)?
Answer: Colleges and universities the United States use an approach called "holistic admissions". This considers all factors that a university considers important, not just academic success. There is literally no GPA, SAT score, or number of AP tests that will guarantee you admission to any particular competitive university, and a scholarship that will cover all or most of your costs is incredibly unlikely. It's probably reasonable to study for one term or perhaps even even one year in an American university, but earning a degree in a foreign country is a luxury, and higher education is more expensive in the US than in any other country.

Question: What is the affordable and best art college university for graphic design in the USA?
Answer: In an unfortunate and odd coincidence, arts colleges are often among the most expensive choices. Art and graphic design programs are available at public colleges and universities, but most of the top ranking programs are at private colleges, and especially art colleges. Again, they seem to charge a lot and offer very little financial aid. Since you would be an international student, even public universities would be expensive. My ballpark low end cost for attending a college or university in the United States as an international student is $30,000 a year, but the number of institutions covered under that is limited and they may not offer graphic design or have a very good program with strong professional opportunities. I think a more realistic cost would be $40,000 a year in this case, and again, that's the low end; attending a private college arts college like RISD or SCAD will probably cost closer to $65,000 a year.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Should I study computer science in a QS 40 rank university or software engineering in aQS 160 ranked university? Also, which would have a better salary and job outlook?
Answer: Well, do you want to study computer science or software engineering. Having been a software engineer and holding a master degree and software engineering, I'm not generally a fan of undergraduate software engineering program, but you should do. I absolutely would not make the decision based upon QS rankings. Focus on what the institution can offer you and how good of a fit it is. These ranking systems are at best rough proxies of some quality, but that is not what opportunities you will experience upon graduation. Outcomes are sometimes factored in (usually looking entirely at salary), but they are certainly not the only thing or primary thing measured. I liken these ranking systems to a ball game, and students aren't players; they are the ball. In addition, looking at the difference in the metrics that would place one university at a rank of 40 and the other at a rank of 160, you'll actually find there isn't much difference.

Question: My professor pulled off my phone from me because I wasn’t paying attention in class. I feel like this is my own business, isn’t?
Answer: I'm generally well liked and not a particularly strict professor, but students quickly learn that there's one thing that they can't do: talk during my class. Oh, don't get me wrong, there are plenty of times for them to talk to each other, but when I am lecturing or (much more often) doing a live programming exercise with the students, they can't have side conversations. Why? It's distracting. Who is it distracting? Me. I'm the professor, and if I'm distracted, then nothing happens in the classroom. You are not allowed to distract me, and the fact that I am paid to be there doesn't change anything. If your professor took your phone away, they are telling you pretty clearly that they believe you are interfering with what needs to happen in that classroom, and no, you're not allowed to do that. Yes, it is your business; you have been politely invited to either behave properly or conduct your business elsewhere.

Question: Can I get financial aid for an associate degree if I'm doing my master's? I'm doing my master's, and I didn't get any financial aid before, but I wanted to go for an associate degree, so do you think I can get financial aid?
Answer: Like others, I'm pretty perplexed. What does "I wanted to go for an associate degree" mean? What's your goal. Do you want to get an associate degree in an unrelated field? Do you want to pursue a vocational associate degree, like dental hygiene? Do you want to do this at the same time as earning your masters degree? These questions are really important because they can impact both the feasibility of the plan and whether or not you get aid. For federal financial aid, you probably will qualify as a second-degree student, and as an independent student by definition, you can take out a fairly large amount in loans. Whether that's a wise idea, I don't know. It would really depend on the specifics of what you're trying to accomplish.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I am currently studying bachelor of business administration, but I think it's getting nowhere and I don't learn anything specific. Do you think it’s better to change my major to computer engineering?
Answer: A few years ago, I was talking to an excellent student during office hours, and I asked her if I would see her in my second semester course the following semester. She told me that she was a business major. I told her that she could easily fix that problem by completing a change of major form. She got the joke and laughed, but she told me that she wanted to stay in business because she didn't have to do any work for any of her courses. I asked her if she really felt that was a good use of her time and energy. She admitted that it didn't sound great when put that way, but I never saw her again… I'm generally opposed to any notion of "good" or "bad" majors, but there are certainly some that concern me. Very high on that list is any business major that does not have extensive quantitative, mathematics, and/or statistical requirements. The focus of many programs seem to be to move as many students as possible through courses without anybody having to actually engage in teaching or learning. I'm not a fan of multiple-choice questions on exams, but they can't have their place. If they are the primary tool of evaluating student learning, I am very concerned. That seems to be the case with many business programs. Now I'm not sure why you're thinking about jumping from business administration to computer engineering. It's a huge leap. I suspect that making that change would require you to effectively start over, leaving you with four years of coursework ahead of you. But if computer engineering is what your heart wants, it's a great field. If not, I think there's a middle ground between business administration and computer engineering. Start thinking of careers that might interest you. If you haven't been to the career center, you should fix that problem ASAP. You can also look at My Next Move, which is a free tool for career exploration from the US Department of Labor.[1] Look at jobs in zones four and five. Want to know what career is interest you, you can start to learn what majors will help you develop the necessary skills. I always recommend students look on LinkedIn, because they're often shocked at the undergraduate field of study of people who hold jobs that interest them.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Why do many people argue that *most* people in the world should not choose a college simply for its prestige? Aren’t most people in the world from Asia, wherein college prestige confers crucial benefits to one’s social status?
Answer: I don’t generally write about “most people in the world.” I might not qualify every answer I write, but I hope it’s generally apparent that a guy from the US knows much more about the US than elsewhere. I have no advice for someone living in Asia, unless they have interest in coming to the US. I will answer this from that perspective. Well, because (if nothing else) most people can’t attend the most prestigious institutions. There are too few seats and too many applicants. Now what does prestige get you in the US? Sure, a degree from MIT makes it easier to get an interview, but we should be comparing like with like. If you were competitive for MIT, you are not going to be at CSUMB. You will likely end up at another prestigious college or university. Maybe not as prestigious, but a degree from a state flagship will still open plenty of doors. But I think the bigger issue is fit. Your future will be decided on the basis of what you can do and what demonstrations you have that you of those skills. In short, more than anything else, your work decides your future. CSUMB grads have placed into the most competitive employers and graduate programs. Fit will decide your growth. It’s not just a question of how far along a skill curve you are, but also what skills you have. And even within a skillset, there are variations; the ability to solve mathematics problems and the ability to perform mental arithmetic are separate. It’s entirely possible good at one and not the other. But going back to my first point about access, too many students commit their emotional welfare to getting into their “dream college.” Then they don’t get in, and they’re miserable. I recall a young woman on Quora bemoaning having been forced to attend the University of Virginia, rather than an Ivy. If MIT seems like a great fit and you can get admitted, great, go. They’ll make it affordable. For the other 99.996% of American students who don’t get into MIT (they admit about 1,275 against about 2.34 million new college freshman), life will go on. And if you get into MIT and you don’t think it’s a fit… MIT and similar schools have an ongoing problem with suicide, but you probably won’t be one of the students who attempts that. However, you may get little value or pleasure out of your education. As I’ve noted countless times, most MIT engineering grads are in fairly quotidian engineering jobs. They worked much, much harder in college than many of their peers in similar or identical roles. Many of them found much of the work miserable… and it didn’t get them further.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What should I do as an undergraduate student in a university around 2000th world ranking to get to a university like MIT, Caltech, Stanford, etc. when I graduate from my current university?
Answer: You should do absolutely nothing to get into one of these universities. You should develop an excellent understanding of your field and have demonstrations of your expertise. You should do that whether or not you want to attend one of the most competitive institutions for postgraduate study. You should do so even if you don’t intend to pursue postgraduate study. Actually, there is something you should do, or rather not do: do not set your expectations inappropriately. The issue isn’t that you’re attending a lower-ranking university (although that can be a factor); the issue is that these institutions turn away the majority of well-qualified students. There is a large luck factor in admission (not so much pure chance as being the right person in the right place at the right time, factors outside of your control). And further, at the postgraduate level, don’t assume that a specific institution is revered in all areas. This is especially important for PhDs. The top programs are not necessarily where you think they will be.

Question: What are the job opportunities for a MFA Dance graduate as an international student in USA?

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I know it is a cartoon and not meant to be taken seriously, but in the cartoon "Invincible", a robot uses electromagnetic couplings instead of bolts. What are real-world examples of electromagnetic connections replacing traditional bolts?
Answer: Bolts aren’t quite as permanent as rivets, but I can’t imagine a bolt being used for something that would frequently be opened. An electromagnetic fastener/solenoid/couple could be used to keep a door closed, but a bolt would not, since it would be very difficult to open the door. Meanwhile, it would be very easy to open the door held in place electronmagnetically, but it would be difficult to ensure that it stayed closed. So if we’re just talking about coupling two things together (and not things like power transmission), you’d use a bolt if you never or rarely wanted to separate the two things and an electromagnet if you frequently wanted to separate the two things. The bolt fails closed, and the electromagnet fails open.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can I apply for PhD with a first class Bachelor's in Chemistry and a PGDip in Chemistry with medicinal chemistry? Due to worsening health, I flunked my resists as well, what can I do to increase my chances of getting into a good funded PhD?
Answer: The problem with applying for a PhD program in the US is that you will be expected to report all of your prior academic work. I suspect that your failed exams will become apparent. It seems very unlikely that a PhD program would take the risk of admitting a student who had failed exams, especially when they failed them twice. A first in chemistry at the bachelor’s level will allay some concerns, but even so, I think you would look like a high-risk student. PhD programs have plenty of applicants who present no significant risk. I should say that I am not in chemistry. I can’t imagine that a chemistry department would be more willing to take a risk, but I don’t know.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is it ethical to use LLM tools to help produce code that is the basis for research if the use thereof is disclosed in the publication, e.g., asking an LLM to produce a small script for filtering data?
Answer: I’m completely revising this response. What I wrote was overly vague, and I hadn’t correctly interpreted the question. My overall “take” is that if the work done by an LLM is significant enough to need to be disclosed, it’s at least concerning. We don’t expect authors to disclose that they used Grammarly in producing a manuscript. It’s one of many tools that can help people communicate better. There are better and worse uses of Grammarly, but in the general sense, it’s innocuous. LLMs seem to help some developers (and researchers) accelerate their workflows. If nothing else, LLMs can interactively offer help and explanation. Even if the code and explanations are not correct, the process of using them that way will make problems less likely; the programmer isn’t treating the generated code as a black box. And code that doesn’t actually analyze data isn’t really a concern; it’s usually fine to not fully understand code that connects to a database (one example given below). But I’ve seen evidence that many researchers are doing what students often do, which is to have ChatGPT or another LLM generate work wholesale. There are even published scholarly articles (not in reputable venues*) that begin with text like, “As a large language model, I can’t…”. Where is the line? I don’t think that’s clear, but if the code at hand is actively manipulating data, I think it’s reasonable to at least double-check the work (so someone other than the person who generated code should review it). If it’s short enough, the time involved is trivial. If it’s more complicated and it manipulates data, then the need for review increases. *- This is honestly probably a No True Scotsman argument, but I don’t think it’s unreasonable to say that a venue will lose all respect when it publishes work that was clearly, unequivocally produced by an LLM.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What would convince any U.S. public high school teacher to teach a summer class on campus every year, aside from obviously earning extra money for doing so? My (now retired) high school chemistry teacher did this for 25 summers.
Answer: A former colleague of mine, a college professor, worked multiple summers. He was not teaching; he was a line cook at a local state park. He did it to help pay for his daughter’s college. Summer school does not typically last all summer, and summer breaks used to be a bit longer. The pay can be good, it might gain a person some pension advantage, and most people I know who teach for a living actually enjoy the job. I suspect that there is less bureaucracy and micromanagement during the summer. However, why not reach out to your high school chemistry teacher and ask them? That way you'll know their specific reason.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is GitHub Copilot free for students?
Answer: I’ll pile on Jeff’s answer. I have a student researcher who is using it for development on a website. We’re all pretty much novices with using this stack, and the website isn’t the research, so I don’t care (in this instance). But… I asked this student to build some code based on some other, working code. Instead of doing so manually, they asked copilot to write the code. Copilot wrote the code, but it didn't work and it didn't leave any trace in the logs, making it difficult for this student to debug. After a few days of banging their head against the desk, they reached out to me for help. I was able to solve the problem in a few minutes, not because I know more, but because I have debugging and reasoning skills that you can't develop if you get someone or something else to write the code. It's very common for computer science (and other) students to experience a powerful but false sense of comprehension; they will tell their professors that they "understand" a given topic, but simply can't implement it. Of course, they don't understand it; if they did, they would be able to implement it. We gain our understanding through implementation and use, not the other way around. Jeff has written before about how this sense of understanding is seductive and destructive. We see the same thing here. Of course copilot is attractive to students, and it might not feel wrong; how is it different from tab completion or even copying code from stack overflow (yes, we know you do this too)? The answer is that the code is worthless regardless of whether or not it runs, because you didn't write it, you don't understand it (if you did, you would've written it), and you definitely can't fix it when something goes wrong. I suspect that my student researcher will continue to use copilot for this web work. Again, because it's not the research itself, I don't really care; the whole point of this is to learn. Sometimes we learn by repeatedly making mistakes until we truly understand why those actions are mistakes. Truly intelligent people aren't the ones who figure things out at first glance; they are the ones who are able to learn from painful lessons that other people go through.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: My sophomore year of Computer Science is approaching. Should I be mentally prepared for all-nighters?
Answer: Eh, probably. Others will point out that an all-nighter is invariably a failure in planning and time management, and they're correct. But it's pretty unusual for a sophomore to have good time management skills. When you're 19 or 20 years old, one all nighter isn't going to destroy your health or ability to function, and you'll hopefully learn through the experience. The best lesson to learn is to plan properly and not have all nighters, but there is something to be said for learning to work under pressure and learning to work when you are exhausted and don't want to work. In fact, the experience of an all nighter can help you develop Better time management and study habits. In addition, most people feel a sense of accomplishment when they complete a project or paper over all nighter. We could argue that it's a false sense of accomplishment, but I don't think it matters much.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can I raise my unweighted GPA back up from a 3.871 to a 4.0? I had a 4.0 freshman year and a 3.871 sophomore year. I just started junior year. I’m not sure what my weighted GPA is but I’m an AP and honors student.
Answer: First, you need to learn how to calculate your GPA. As you've noticed, it's a useful skill. As Michael Scheele points out, all of the mathematics involved should be things that you have not only learned, but be comfortable with. If you aren't, this is a great way to relearn. Second, as you've hopefully discovered by now, you can't have a 4.0 unweighted cumulative GPA, but that's not important for two reasons: it's not usually a major in admission decisions and (more importantly) the hard part will be figuring out how to bring your grades up. Focus on that.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Which country do you think would become democratic first in our lifetime, Russia or China?
Answer: I agree with Tomaž, but my reasoning is a bit different. I don't see China as fascist; I see China as China. It's not communism, it's not capitalism, it's just China. I think they are more likely to become a democracy first because I think there's a strong likelihood that China will fracture overtime. I don't think it's going to be a violent civil war with hundreds of millions of deaths, but I think that eventually we will find that "the center cannot hold." At that point, some of the states could easily find their way to something resembling democracy.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Hi I’m an undergraduate international student in the USA with an F-1 visa, and I already had a degree before coming but I wanted to get another, but now I want to get my masters done with my previous degree, can I get a transfer to another school?
Answer: I'm not sure what "get my masters done with my previous degree" means, but it doesn't matter: go talk to your DSO.
