Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Does Kamala's promise of price controls show that she has no understanding of basic supply and demand?
Answer: There are price controls and price controls, and there are consequences and consequences. During the pandemic, some people drove around the country buying bottles of hand sanitizer and boxes of facemasks and attempted to sell them for outrageous prices. Many of them violated multiple state and federal laws, and if they were lucky they only had their stock confiscated. Those laws are price controls, and at the time, nobody other than the perpetrators complained. That doesn't mean that all price controls are good; only an idiot would point to a good example and claim that no bad examples could exist, or vice versa. We live in a world in which there are many mechanisms to control prices, most of which we don't even really notice.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Does taking more A levels subjects make you a more competitive applicant to US universities? BTW I take maths, further maths, physics, biology, chemistry and economics, and plan to primarily apply to IS universities.
Answer: No. Remember that US colleges and universities use a holistic admission, so even if we could call this "more academic success", it's not as valuable as demonstrating other qualities that these institutions are looking for. Also, do you have the money to study in the United States? A low-end estimate of costs is about $30,000 a year for each of four years, and a high-end estimate of $100,000 per year.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: After completing my graduation, can I get a full-time job as an international student with MFA in Dance degree in USA?
Answer: I'm a bit confused by the question. If you are actually a student and presumably on an F-1 visa, you can only work part time during academic terms. Unless your MFA program offers you an assistantship with support (which is typically done for being a course instructor), the jobs available to you will be campus jobs, often making minimum wage or not much more. There is no way to earn enough money to live off of working like this, and especially not to earn enough to live and pay tuition fees. Once you graduate, you will qualify for OPT, but you need to find an employer who is willing to employ you for up to one year, and the job has to be directly related to your field of study. It couldn't even be in something like music; it would have to be in dance. After that one year of OPT, you would need an employment visa, and you aren't going to get one of those if you aren't a world-class dancer.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Quitting my Ph.D program in Applied Experimental psychology at Central Michigan despite a December 2024 graduation b/c I'm anxious due to the university cutting all psychology Ph.D programs soon and budget issues as a whole. How do I tell my advisor?
Answer: You and I have had a number of interactions, and I've done my best to encourage you to reconsider quitting. I think you know that I agree with the answers here that say you are making a mistake. It doesn't matter if you do a good job or bad job, as long as you get the degree. If you have absolutely dedicated to quitting, drop your advisor an email and be done with it. I suspect your reasoning is that you simply cannot afford the emotional cost of completing. I don't know if there is anything that anybody can say to convince you otherwise, but I suspect with the emotional cost of not finishing will be worse. You are stuck between a rock and a hard place, but this is a common enough scenario in life that we have that aphorism for it. The situation isn't as dire as you fear; the anxiety is making it feel dire, because that's what anxiety does. Since you are just writing at this point, with maybe a little data analysis, the solution to your problem is also what you need to do if you quit, which is to place yourself in a very supportive community. If you find that community, you can make it through the dissertation. If you don't, I strongly suspect that quitting the dissertation is going to not going to alleviate your anxiety, at least not in the long run. For now, tell your advisor that you're busy dealing with personal problems, or just problems in general. Tell them not to expect to hear from you for a couple of weeks. In the meantime, figure out how you're going to find and sustain supportive community that you need. This is work that you need to do working with the mental health services you have access to at the moment.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I scored 272 in the GRE. How many hours of preparation do I need to study daily to score 300?
Answer: There’s no way to answer that question, and it’s not even the right question. Without knowing the breakdown of your scores, we don’t know precisely how to interpret them, but a general interpretation is that you are near the bottom of students who have taken the GRE. If English is not your first language and you haven’t recently studied or used mathematics and you didn’t familiarize yourself with the exam ahead of time, then it might be worthwhile retaking. However, if all three of those don’t all apply to you, I don’t think you’re going to do very well on the GRE in the long run. Here’s my recommendation: get a Princeton review or similar GRE practice book, spend about three to five hours each day for the next two weeks reviewing the material, and then take one of the practice tests. If your score is not dramatically higher, I don’t think it’s going to improve enough to make a difference. You can spread that time out over longer than a couple of weeks, but you do need between 30 and 60 hours of study time to get a reasonable diagnostic score. A final note: don’t combine the GRE scores. Each score (verbal, quantitative, and analytical writing) stands on its own. The percentile scales of the verbal and quantitative scores are dramatically different, even though they are on the same numeric scale. When you report your scores to people before you ask for information, give the verbal and quantitative scores separately.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is Biden's camp losing luster for not being able to win the Olympic gold medal tally by a far cry when compared with China? A result of poor administration then.
Answer: It's fairly common for Americans to take pride in our country, but that can cut two ways. Yes, we can become be upset when we don't do as well on some sort of international stage as we might have hoped, but we just focus on something in which we are doing very well. I think there are three areas where Americans genuinely become concerned if we don't have medalists: women's gymnastics, swimming, and men's basketball. For the most part, we just enjoy the competitions and will readily cheer on stellar athletes (and a lot of personality) regardless of the country.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I have a 39 IB predicted score. Converting it into GPA gets me 3.8 UW and 4.6 W. I am expecting a mid 1400s SAT score. What are my chances for UC San Diego?
Answer: I'd guess near zero. First, you haven't calculated your GPA correctly. The University of California system has its own rules, and they only count grades from courses taken during the second and third year high school. Second, the fact that you didn't know this (which is NOT representative of some sort of huge character flaw on your part) indicates that you aren't from California. That dramatically reduces your chances of admission. Third, if you aren't from California, the cost of UC San Diego will be outrageous, on the order of $65,000 a year. Little or no need-based or merit aid will be available to you. Even if someone were willing to loan you the necessary amount, you would be foolish to take it. For a while, my "dream college" was UC Santa Cruz. The costs were much lower at the time, even adjusted for inflation, but I didn't even apply. There was no way that it would make financial sense. Fortunately, college is four years followed by decades in which you will have more freedom. I now live about 45 minutes south of Santa Cruz and go up there frequently. If I really wanted to, there's a decent chance I could get a job at UC Santa Cruz, and have them pay me money, instead of the other way around.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How bad does getting teeth fillings hurt? I was just told today that I’d have to get many and it’d probably take 2-4 appointments. I’m young and never had dental work done. before. I’m really scared about the pain and I want to know what to expect.
Answer: For me, by far the most uncomfortable part is sitting with my mouth open for 30 minutes to an hour. There's some pain with the Novocain injections (although less than their used to be; my dentist now uses a topical anesthetic on the gums and slowly injects Novocain to reduce pain. I do feel some pain during the drilling (some people do, some people don't) and my jaw tends to be achy afterward, but that's primarily from keeping my mouth open. They put blocks between your teeth to keep your jaw open, but it's still uncomfortable. But like many medical and dental treatments, you're saving yourself a lot of pain down the road. Other than routine cleaning and a review of teeth and gum health, having a cavity filled is the least painful dental procedure. Trust me, you're going to be fine. Uncomfortable, but fine.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How can I be accepted to Yale Young Global Scholars program? Right now I am 16 years old, recently finished grade 9. In my school we don't take IGCSE as we directly take AS and A level exams. I haven't taken my SAT yet. Also, I want to study medicine
Answer: Before you worry too much about it, realize that these programs are “enrichment“ programs; they are not designed that you into Yale (or any other college or university). While they are somewhat competitive, their primary concern is that you can pay the fees.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: If humanity be extinct and another intelligent creature arise, it too would discover the same Platonic solids were fundamental forms exist waiting to be discovered. Is this example sufficient to demonstrate that ideas exist separately from the mind?
Answer: One frustrating fact in both philosophy and psychology is that we only have one model of intelligence. We don’t know what else intelligence could look like. Many science fiction fans and reviewers comment on how often aliens look like humans, but think how rarely we see different kinds of sentence and perception. Platonic solids are just a collection of shapes that meet certain rules. Like all other provable parts of math, they aren't subjected. Mathematics is a conceptual model of both real world phenomena and derived rules, a language that follows absolute rules, but it doesn't mean that there couldn't be two possibly very different languages that follow the same set of rules. How a non-human intelligence might conceptualize these same rules and qualifying shapes is not something we can predict.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What do you think would have been the "best alternative" or the least damaging alternative for Alan Turing after his 1952 trial which was a dead end: prison or the harmful chemical castration he eventually underwent?
Answer: While as a concept it's horrifying and I would never defend it, I think your framing is a bit dramatic. Turing was placed on DES for one year, during which he experienced both a loss of libido and some unpleasant body changes. However, this is often cited as a primary motive for his suicide. There are a couple of problems with that. First, while the inquest concluded suicide, there was no note and there are reasonable explanations for how Turing came to accidentally ingest suicide (he was working with it in his research and had been for a while). We will never know one way or the other. Second, he had been off of DES for over a year when he died. The obvious solution is to decriminalize homosexuality, and that did happen, even if not in time to prevent Turing from coming to harm. What would have happened had Turing not accepted the chemical castration treatment and instead was sent to prison? We can't possibly know.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is Tim Walz responsible for spending over $100,000.00 to put tampons and feminine napkins in school boys bathrooms? Talk about weird.
Answer: If he did, I want him by my side when I buy my next car. Google says that there are about 2,000 public schools in Minnesota. That’s $50 per school. Ok, they aren’t required in elementary schools. Let’s say $100. Walz’s job as Governor is to faithfully execute the laws passed by the Minnesota State Legislature. Yes, he signed the bill into law (although this isn't exactly what the law dictated). But his primary job is to oversee the law being enacted. If he furnished 1,000 or so schools with tampons and pads for just $100 per school, he drives excellent bargains. Procurement in public schools is not generally very effective.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Why does the Constitution lay out only three requirements to serve as president: A natural-born citizen At least 35 years old A resident of the U.S. for at least 14 years. No basic qualifications or experience required for any low level position?
Answer: Well, and they must be elected. That’s kind of how a republican, representative democracy works. Regardless of the imperfections of the system, we choose our leaders more or less directly. I think it's generally preferable to have as few restrictions as possible. Harry Truman was a failed businessman who only briefly attended college. He had limited political experience when he landed on the Democratic ticket in 1944, and the leaders of the Democratic Party seemed to be surprisingly unaware that they were pretty much handing this guy the presidency. He was one of the greatest presidents of the 20th century, and really in American history. Dick Nixon was brilliant, incredibly successful, and certainly didn't enter politics to make money. He was… not a great president. What requirements would you impose on the presidency, and how would they benefit us? I often see people suggest requirements that would exclude somebody they don't like, but that's not a reason to have that rule.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Should I double major in criminal Justice and journalism?
Answer: Probably not. Both journalism and criminal justice are popular “career” majors, in the sense that many students choose them because they think that the major leads to a career. In both cases, it doesn’t work. Journalism is a real career, but it’s a terrible career for employment opportunities. I’d guess that there are over 100 would-be journalists, people actively working as part-time freelancers and stringers, for every full-time (semi-) permanent journalism job, and such jobs are disappearing. As for criminal justice, it's a very popular major for people who want to go into law enforcement, but if you don't want to go into law enforcement, probably a bad choice, and it's not necessary for law-enforcement jobs. Law schools do not like criminal justice or legal studies majors; they don't consider either program to academically rigorous or really relevant to what lawyers do. (Note that I am not passing judgment; I'm just sharing what law schools think.)

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Was it a normal practice in 1980s to shutdown a personal computer by just simply pressing the power button? Would that damage the computers at that time?
Answer: I’ll go one step further with a slight alteration: it was normal to flip the power switch. Computers don’t have power switches anymore (ignoring the switch on the power supply of more traditional desktop/tower computers). At least, most of them don’t. They have what are called “soft power” buttons. These are buttons that send it interrupt telling the computer to shut down. In fact, part of a computer built in recent decades never actually shuts down unless power is lost completely (the computer is unplugged and the battery is dead if a laptop) AND any motherboard battery is removed or otherwise dead. I can’t pinpoint when soft power buttons became the norm and we started referring to the other kind as “hard power“ buttons or switches. My first computer (Commodore 64) had a switch. Flipping the switch didn’t send an interrupt; it literally cut the power. It's not completely true that immediately cutting the power to a device cannot do any damage. As some of the answers here indicate, unsaved data can be lost, and that can even render system unusable. In addition, anything with moving parts could be damaged. That doesn't necessarily mean that it will be. In particular, data drives are sensitive. Ideally, hard drive heads would be parked (removed from the platter and placed in inappropriate positions so that the hard drive can be moved without risk). There were tricks to make this more likely to happen; a hard drive could have a capacitor that would store enough energy and control logic to immediately park the head properly using that last bit of energy when power was cut. This is not a major problem now, but was in the past.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I'm graduating from a computer science major and I got a 3.2 GPA. Is that a good score?
Answer: Look, anything above a 2.0 is "good", because anything below 2.0 means that you don't get your degree. The difference between somebody with a degree and someone without a degree is much larger than the difference between a 2.0 and a 4.0. So far, so good. The problem with your GPA is the old joke "that and five dollars will get you a cup of coffee." What really matters is not your GPA but how much prep work you have done for your career. Since you concern is your GPA, I have to assume that the answer is "very little." Unfortunately, your timing is awful; there have been few internship opportunities in the past couple of years, and the job market doesn't look to improve for this coming Spring. Even so, there are things that you can do to advance your career opportunities. The changing market doesn't give you an excuse for inaction; it demands more serious and earlier action. So anyway, get started with the stuff below ASAP. And by ASAP, I mean today; start by contacting your career center today and get an appointment with a career counselor. You are several years behind, but starting now is much better than starting in a week.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do I tell my parents I’m struggling in school and want to switch schools?
Answer: If you trust your parents, and you probably should, I would recommend starting with the first part: "mom, dad, I'm struggling in school." Maybe write down a few points to help you remember how to describe your struggle. Is it grades? Social Issues? Not feeling like you're learning? Feel like you could do better elsewhere? Once you describe what the issues are to your parents, explain that you feel there's a need for change you can have your suggested outcome, presumably transferring to a different school (perhaps one identified), but your parents may have better advice. Often parents offer this "advice": work harder. It's not ill intention, but it's also not actionable. At that point you can ask, "can you help me with that?" Now if you really feel that the solution is to a particular different school, you should outline why that school is a better choice for you in the short and long terms. Again, write this down before you talk to your parents; just winging it is not a great way for a child convince adults. Don't forget to consider the long-term consequences; an academically less rigorous school might leave you less prepared for the next stage of your academic or professional life. What will you do then?

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I'm an engineering student and have 3.1/4 GPA, IELTS band 7 and my GRE is 300. What American university can I apply to?
Answer: There is no American university I would apply to with those stats. Now I don't know the whole world. Perhaps a degree from an American university is inherently valuable. I can assure you that some institution will admit you for some program; masters degree students are a huge source of income for universities across the US. However, I seriously question whether that degree would hold any value on the job market. If you have $60,000 or more to spend on a US degree, by all means do so. Don't expect it to have good practical value.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What are the common mistakes international students make when applying to Ivy League universities for a scholarship?
Answer: By far the most common mistake international students make is applying in the first place. Nobody likes to hear this, but the odds are so heavily stacked against you that you're probably wasting time and money. Yes, you may be able to get an application fee waiver, but countless international students spend hundreds of dollars that they don't have on things like SAT tests and WES transcript reviews. Less than 1% of international applicants are admitted. Few anre even seriously considered, and you would already know if you were likely to be in that group because people in your home country with expertise in the matter would be guiding your academic career. Something similar happens to students who apply to less competitive institutions. They get admitted, and if it's a private college or university, they get a huge scholarship: 50% off! They think that they are halfway to attending , but in reality, virtually every student gets that same discount, and the other 50% is effectively impossible to "find" if your family cannot afford it and you cannot get loans in your home country. A good low end estimate for the cost of attending college or university in the United States is $30,000 a year. That can rise quickly if you want to attend a university you've heard of or live in a place you've heard of. So these students get their hopes up, only to find that they have hit a wall and have no effective means to get the amount of money they are expected to pay.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Since aerospace engineers build from scratch private jets, then which job title designs the private jet to begin with just like how architects designs the buildings?
Answer: Car designs are initially proposed by somebody with the job title of car or automotive designer. That person probably has engineering training, but they may not be an engineer. A car design is just a series of sketches or (more commonly now) 3-D model. It doesn't need to do anything. That design will be refined before a physical car ever takes shape. Much of that refinement is done by engineers. If you've ever seen a car go from a concept car at an auto show to a production model, a number of changes are necessary for safety, practicality, accessibility, and affordability. The reason that supercars can look so outrageous that they don't really need to be practical in the way that a Ford or Toyota has to be. Similarly, an architect will sketch out a building, but if it's sufficiently complicated, civil engineers will be critical to making that building a reality. The finished building won't perfectly match the first sketches. but there isn't an equivalent for aircraft. Cars are lumps of metal that sit on the ground and move. Aerodynamics are important, but there's a lot of room left for "style". Buildings are lumps of metal, concrete, wood, and glass, and aren't supposed to move very much; there are big engineering demands, but again, there's a lot of room for art. This is much less true with aircraft. Aircraft have to move through the air, and every shape decision impacts how that happens. There are aircraft designers, but everyone with a significant impact on the design of an aircraft will be from an engineering background. The only part of the aircraft where that's not true is inside; there are specialized interior designers who work on aircraft cabins. Boats and ships are designed by naval architects, but naval architecture is an engineering discipline. It could easily be called naval engineering. There's a related discipline, marine engineering, which deals with shipboard systems and other things that operate on and in water. But yeah, with aircraft and spacecraft, there just isn't much room for exterior style. There may be accents, but the basic design of everything other than the cabin is dictated by physics, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, materials science, and industrial engineering.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How beneficial is it to pursue education until a PhD for an industrial career?
Answer: In a small number of fields, pursuing a PhD can open some doors that would otherwise be closed without also closing some doors. For example, someone with a PhD in computer science (if their research skills were exceptional and aligned with the work of the company) get a research job at a private company. Until recently, someone with a CS PhD and the right problem-solving skills could also get a software engineering job, often starting at a higher level than new hires without post graduate degrees. Beyond that, a PhD is rarely the best way to maximize your earnings. Yes, there are some people in industry research in many fields, some of whom are very well paid, but with few exceptions, someone who earned a PhD could have chosen a more financially rewarding career path that required less education.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do I decide my A-level subjects? I am a private student so I do not have access to career counselling. I am unsure what to pursue in my further studies.
Answer: First, while it is unfortunate that you do not have access to career counseling through your an academic institution, such counseling doesn’t need to be formal. I can’t speak to the United Kingdom, but I can also tell you that in the United States, local job offices (in our case, run by the county) can offer assistance and would typically be very happy to. See if you can find a resource, and if not, start contacting people. Ask your parents or other working adults to help you connect with professionals. Create an account on LinkedIn and try to find local professionals in careers that interest you. In the meantime, start by looking at university courses that interest you, and see which A-levels they require. Make a spreadsheet. You can try to pick the levels that are both most appropriate for your abilities and interest and also most relevant for the courses that interest you. I don’t know the timeline for your decision, but I would encourage you to spend serious time choosing wisely. One of the problems that I have with the UK system is that it is not particularly flexible. It is not easy to change your studies later. Better to slow down and make good decisions than to rush into unwise choices.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Which United States university is the most likely for a biochemistry major international student applicant to be given a full-ride scholarship?
Answer: There is no such university. Such scholarships are exceptionally competitive. While there are a handful of universities that will admit international students without considering whether or not they need financial aid and will then fully fund their admitted students, admission to one of those institutions requires being truly extraordinary, one of the best students in your country, and best has to be measured objectively (things like National and international rewards).

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How can get funds to raise my tuition for masters? I'm doing masters in Electrical Engineering. But am financially down and I cant raise my tuition. My laptop is broken, I don't have money to repair it. I'm looking a out for help.
Answer: The typical cost for a master’s degree in engineering in the United States starts at about $60,000 (including two years of tuition fees and living expenses. The upper bound of costs is well more than twice that. If you are an international student, you must have one year of costs at hand to get a visa. They’re simply isn’t an amount of hustle” that will get you this kind of money. If you are an American, you will almost certainly take out federal and private loans. If you are an international student, you need to arrange funding in your home country before applying for a visa. If you are a truly exceptional student, you can apply for a Fulbright scholarship. The US grants about 4000 of those a year.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can a student with a lower grade and good extra curriculum get into MIT? What do you consider a good extracurricular? Can you suggest me some as I have interest in computer and maths?
Answer: Fortunately, MIT will not admit a student without strong grades. Nor would that student want to be admitted; MIT has an incredibly rigorous core undergraduate STEM education, and that student has effectively no chance of success in it. That’s before getting to demanding coursework necessary to complete the degree. If MIT is your “dream school”, this is yet another example of why “dream schools” are such a terrible idea. It would be a nightmare… but again, it won’t happen. You should further understand that an applicant with very strong grades and “good extracurriculars” also stands no chance of admission. There’s no set of menu options that leads to any university with a 5% acceptance rate. Finally, you don’t need to go to MIT. Go where you get in and then be excellent.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can I get admissions in good universities (undergraduate) in USA and Canada with good academic records and 7bands?
Answer: Sure, depending on how you defined good university, of course. But here’s a question for you: do you have the $30,000-$100,000 a year it will cost to attend a college or university in the US? If not, then admission is irrelevant.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How likely is my student to be admitted to Ivy League colleges this year?
Answer: Near zero. I’m not looking at stats. If your child was a legacy or a DI-level athlete, you’d have mentioned that or (more likely) not asked the question in the first place. Those 5–7% acceptance rates make the Ivies seem much more accessible than they really are.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What is harder to successfully complete in and why; medical school for aspiring doctors or flight school for aspiring pilots?
Answer: The reason these two things can’t readily be compared is that you are comparing one thing that happens at the very beginning of an education and one thing that happens as the culmination of an education. I’ll just write about the US here. For the moment, let’s ignore the required health and vision tests for pilots. It’s not particularly hard to get a private pilot license. You start from scratch and learn to fly. It’s a lot more work than getting a drivers license, but it requires just forty hours of flight time and can be completed in a couple of months. Getting to a commercial flight license takes 250 hours of flight time. Meanwhile, to begin medical school in the US, you must have a bachelor’s degree and compete for a limited number of spots; far less than half of all medical school applicants ever get admitted. Medical school is a very demanding four year program. That is followed by a residency that takes at least three years, and only after the residency are you allowed to practice independently. If we think in terms of education as an adult beginning after high school, “flight school“ can be completed in the following summer to get as far as a PPL, and a single year to get a CFL. It can take longer, but it doesn’t have to. By comparison, an undergraduate degree and medical school take a combined eight years, and you still aren’t a fully licensed physician at the end of that. We should consider two more things: military flight school and ATP (airline transport pilot) licenses. Military school has a high washout rate. There isn’t really a way to know who will be successful ahead of time, and the military isn’t really bothered by a washout rate. Those washouts become officers serving in other areas. I don’t think it’s fair to say that it’s easy to get into military pilot program, but it certainly easier than it is to get into medical school. In contrast, virtually all of the students who enter medical school will become licensed physicians, because there is extensive vetting ahead of time (which is what makes it harder to get into military flight school). Completing an airline transport pilot license and (potentially, if things work out) eventually becoming a captain or first officer for a major carrier flying Boeing or Airbus jets is a long, involved process. It’s a bit closer to the pathway to become a physician, but it’s not really close because there are multiple steps along the way, including either a CFL or military flight training.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Do university professors get to send their own children to the university they work for for free?
Answer: It’s complicated. Generally speaking, more competitive private institutions offer more tuition benefits, but there are a few universals. This answer will be for US; I can’t speak to other countries. First, most of these programs (if not all) are available to the children of any full-time faculty or staff at the institution. However, universities often contract with private companies, and the people employed by those companies would generally not be covered. Some institutions offer nothing. Some offer a token amount (I believe I qualify for a few hundred dollars a semester for me or a relative). Some colleges offer free tuition at only that institution. Some colleges are in consortia in which the children of faculty and staff can attend any institution in the consortium for free (or heavily discounted). I believe some of these limit the number of such students who can attend each institution each year, so it may be competitive. Some colleges offer free tuition anywhere in the US or even the world, usually capped only by whatever that institution charges. I believe that the University of Chicago still does this, which leads me to believe that most of the self-styled “elite” institutions offer something comparable, too. They certainly have the money to do so. Public colleges and universities are restricted by state law, so benefits tend to be limited or nonexistent.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What might it indicate if a child almost always stutters when speaking to their parents but speaks normally with everyone else?
Answer: Could it indicate a child who is afraid of their parents? Sure. Could it be a sign of abuse? Sure. Is it necessarily the case? No. There’s nothing we can know or meaningfully infer from this one piece of information.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is it acceptable to offer services/commissions for students to complete their projects, such as set plans, thesis, & assignments? If not, what types of commissions are permissible for archi-students without violating any legal or ethical guidelines?"
Answer: Generally speaking, offering academic work to be presented under another person’s name is incredibly unethical. If it’s submitted in a professional context, it may be fraud (which is unethical and illegal). There are circumstances where it’s generally considered OK; many famous people “write” autobiographies, etc., that are really ghostwritten. But the exceptions are rare, and certainly wouldn’t apply to student work.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Do Texas A&M university and University of Texas of Austin Texas let international students pay in-state tuition fees if they get more than 1000$ or 4000$ of scholarship? Is it possible for international student to receive that much of scholarship?
Answer: I’d be surprised if UT Austin did this. I checked and this is basically a law saying that Texas public colleges and universities can waive out-of-state tuition for students who have certain levels of merit-based scholarship. Can does not mean does, and the money from international students is valuable. As for getting the scholarship in the first place, it’s going to be difficult. You should assume that this is not possible.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: If I have a master's degree in IT and a bachelor's in a non-IT field, can I just put my master's in my resume as I'm applying for an IT job?
Answer: Can you? Sure. Should you? Probably not. People will notice and they’ll wonder why. It’s not uncommon for someone to have switched to computing for graduate programs (I did). It’s not surprising or alarming, and I’ve actually had quite a few interesting discussions during interviews about my undergrad degree in the humanities.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is there a high ranked, good university in the U.S. with low tuition fees for international students or gives good scholarships to international students?
Answer: How do you define “low tuition fees”? A good approximation of the lowest possible cost of attendance is about $30,000 per year. That is not for a college that you have ever heard of or in a location that will excite you. If you are truly extraordinary, there are colleges that will offer scholarships. If you have multiple national or international awards, for example. But if you had that kind of background, you wouldn’t be asking.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What can I do to get caught up on my school work if I miss the first week of high school?
Answer: I had a bright student who, for personal reasons, failed a class I taught. I knew they were capable of success. The next semester, they retook the class. They had planned a trip during the semester. I wanted to tell them that it was obvious that this was a vacation and that it was a terrible idea, but this is an adult who does not need my permission. They did ask my advice on how to succeed. I told them. They didn’t do it, or rather, didn’t do enough of it. They failed and could not continue in the computer science major. I hope they had a lot of fun on their trip… This occurred in college, not high school. You’ll be fine if you do what your teachers say. And I mean everything. Otherwise…

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What are some teaching jobs that pay for graduate school?
Answer: That’s (generally) not how it works. You get into a grad program (typically a PhD) that offers you an assistantship, which gives you a tuition waiver, stipend, and subsidized health insurance in exchange for teaching or research work. Some K-12 schools offer teachers some amount of money to pursue master’s degrees in education, but I’m told that’s now rare.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Will India be able to become a big IT hub by 2035?
Answer: India is a big IT hub. All of the major international tech companies have offices, and Tata Consultancy Services is a major player in IT globally.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I just finished high school and will be starting college next month. I'm unsure whether to choose networking, software engineering, or web development for a better future career?
Answer: Those are presumably concentrations within a computer science degree. Assuming that’s correct, it’s probably 4–5 different courses you choose in your junior and senior year. Nothing to worry about now. All offer excellent futures for some and no futures for some. The key is to work hard, learn, and use experiential learning to demonstrate what you learn.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Do civil engineers and architects work towards the same goal of planning new buildings? If yes, why not merge the two areas of study?
Answer: They don’t work toward the same goals. They have different goals. Sometimes those goals align, and sometimes they’re in conflict; what an architect may want may not be safe or might be unreasonable costly. Then they discuss. They have different jobs because they have different training emphasizing these different goals. We can only relate them by stepping back so far that it’s not meaningful to connect them. Both your high school English teachers and mathematics teachers had the same general goal, educating you, but that doesn’t mean that they could cross over.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Does the ranking of a university where one completed his undergraduate matter if one wants to get admitted to a top university like MIT in the future for an MS or PhD?
Answer: Ranking? No. What is potentially important is what the people on the admissions committee think of your institution. But what’s more important than that is what you did there. MIT routinely rejects applicants from MIT, Caltech, Harvey Mudd, Cambridge, IIT, etc., and accepts students from much less prestigious institutions. They know that they’re admitting the student, not the college they used to attend.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: When applying for USA universities, as an American citizen living abroad my whole life, am I considered international with out-of-state tuition?
Answer: So the answer from Lea Fisher is correct: it depends. Some public institutions will consider you an out-of-state US student. Some may consider you an international student. I generally recommend that students in your circumstance find a way to live and work in the US for a year before pursuing college; it can potentially be sufficient to establish in-state residence. You will typically need to be employed. You must look at each state’s regulations for determining in-state student status. Some states have systems that will help you.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What are the eligibility requirements for a Master's Degree scholarship in the USA? How can one secure a full scholarship for a Master's Degree in the USA?
Answer: Be extraordinary, and apply for a Fulbright Fellowship. They give about 4,000 each year. That might sounds like a lot. It’s not. Almost every person earning a master’s degree in the US (including American students) is paying all or the majority of costs of their degree.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is a B.Tech recognized at an Ivy League university like Stanford or MIT?
Answer: OK, since you’ve used the label, the Ivy League is an athletic league, whose sports team compete against each other. Seriously. And neither MIT nor Stanford is part of it. It’s not an equivalent to the Russell Group in the UK. It’s not a list of the best universities. If you’re speaking of the degree from India, sure. But… these institutions receive many well-qualified applicants for every seat in every postgraduate program. You aren’t likely to be admitted. Nobody is likely to be admitted.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: As a professor in a faculty search committee, would you prefer an assistant teaching professor applicant at a no-name university or an engineer with a previous postdoc experience from a top-tier univ. assuming that publications, etc are the same?
Answer: I want an assistant teaching professor who has demonstrated the ability to teach. Prestige is not a measure of teaching ability. Postdocs and publications are not measures of teaching ability. Suppose Candidate A has a PhD from Podunk State, has no publications of note, and has experience as an instructor of record with clear evidence of success and a commitment to growth/improvement. Candidate B does not have teaching experience but has a PhD from MIT and postdocs at CMU and Berkeley. We’re going to hire Candidate A nine times out of ten (the interview does count, but nine times out of ten, A will run circles around B). Is that an absolute? No. But horses for courses.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Will a low grade in English affect my application for engineering for a university?
Answer: What’s low? A D? Yes. A B+? No. And what university? Regional comprehensive university? Less likely to be important if you’ve done well overall. State flagship? Potentially a big issue. An expensive private university where you’d need nearly a full ride? Very big issue.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do I document this? My public high school starts on Monday. Although I have tried to enroll and register for classes, I have none. The administration is uncooperative and my parents are not technologically savvy, not that I am a whiz or anything.
Answer: High schools generally don’t let students self-enroll or self-register for classes. If you are in-district, show up with a parent on Monday morning and ask to enroll. As others indicate, your parent will need some proof of identity for you (typically a birth certificate) and proof of address (there can be ways around this, but if you have these things, save yourself some time). You will be enrolled and will meet with a guidance counselor to get registered for classes. That’s when the hard part begins; who knows what is available? But don’t call. Don’t email. Show up.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Why do companies make you sign up for job apps like indeed? Is this just a scam so they can have your information in some way and get ads and PO-up in your email? Also would they use this like a blacklist to tell other companies about you?
Answer: No. It’s because the system works in their favor; you want a job, they have the job, and so you’ll use a system that’s convenient for them. And the alternative, which isn’t uncommon, is to create a separate account on the corporate system for each company you’re applying for and re-enter all of your data. That’s not more convenient for you. Also, a blacklist or blocklist or whatever you want to call it is a list of people, companies, etc., who are off limits. But you know who does sell information about you and everything you do? And who knows who you are, even if you think that they don’t and you didn’t tell them? Quora. And every other social media site you use.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: As an Australian high school student wanting to study at university in England (in 2026), will my HSC score be accepted or will I need to pursue other similar tests? How much time would I need to apply and what scholarships are available?
Answer: The good news is that some students have already asked this question. The bad news is that, as of this moment, the answers are not available: But it looks like the short answer is “yes, your HSC score will be sufficient”… but for what?

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Does undergraduate school matter for engineering?
Answer: I primarily want to draw attention to what Shane wrote. I’ve watched this world for a while. Talent will out, the cream will rise to the top. Institutions like MIT admit students based on what they’ve achieved by (roughly) age 17. It’s not a perfect proxy for what their futures hold. Even MIT doesn’t think so. Of course, it’s not as simple as that. For the right student, MIT is a place to grow that might not be readily replicated elsewhere. But… it might be. People often believe myths about specialness, and sometimes limited resources can force people to be more inventive. I’ve met plenty of MIT grads, and they’re typically in routine jobs, working alongside a lot of people who didn’t go to MIT. If you forced me to bet on the relative success of two engineers, one from MIT and one from Podunk State University, I’d bet the MIT grad would be more professionally successful. But if I didn’t have to bet, would I? No. It’s not always going to be the case. One answer merged into this question starts by describing a woman who “has an associate’s in hairdressing” as a bad candidate for engineering,[1] but Shane has written about a woman in his grad program, who has a PhD in EE from UIUC, who worked for decades as a hairdresser and didn’t start college until (IIRC) her 40s.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Does aia have department of education license?
Answer: And what is aia? There was a college by the name of Art Institute of Atlanta, part of a chain of for-profit art colleges that are now all closed. But to go a step further, colleges and universities are not licensed by the federal government. They must earn accreditation from one of several private accreditors recognized by the US Department of Education in order to receive federal funds. Some states do some licensure of academic institutions, but again this effectively devolves onto accreditation. For historical reasons, the gold standard for higher education in the US is regional accreditation. The national accreditors do not adhere to the same standards.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What are the overall operational costs for a private and/or public university of over 30,000 students in the United States? Basically, what is the overall cost to run the entire university in a year?
Answer: I think you’re asking for a baseline, like “what’s the real cost?” Interesting question. As institutions grow larger, they tend to have more programs and a larger research profile. Graduate programs, professional schools (especially medical schools), and other programs that are characteristic of a large university drastically increase the budget. While it’s possible to find a small institution with a big budget, it’s going to be difficult to find a large institution with a small budget. Also, campus housing is a big factor. The budget at a commuter school will be lower than a peer with a lot of on-campus housing. This is one reason why community colleges and schools with big online programs have smaller budgets. It can also be misleading, because housing is quite a bit different than educational expenses. Also, as you get to a size of about 20,000+, you start losing any economy of scale. You have more layers of administration and staff. Yes, there are much larger institutions, but even 20,000 students is a big, complex machine. There’s a sweet spot of about 5,000–10,000 students where costs are about as optimal as they can be. I arbitrarily chose Central Michigan University. They have about half as many students, and their annual budget is $443.2 for this coming year. Wayne State University, which has about 25,000 students, has a budget of $1 billion. I don’t know of a way of finding which large university has the lowest operating cost. It’s likely to be a public regional comprehensive in a large but inexpensive city with relatively little on-campus housing. However, there are relatively few states with non-research universities that large. California has some, but it’s California (where everything is absurdly expensive), and the largest CSU campuses produce a lot of research (but can’t directly grant PhDs). A ballpark baseline budget for a school that size is going to be about $1 billion. Upper bound might be 10x that, especially if there is a medical school.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Are there any charity organizations which provide help for university students on emergency funding?
Answer: Every college and university I have been associated with has had multiple emergency funds for different purposes. Local social service organizations often have emergency resources, although they are more focused on things like housing and food than cash. I don't know of any private organization that has money for specifically for students for emergencies, and not being able to pay your tuition is generally not considered an emergency. As a result, most money you might get couldn't be used for that purpose.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Can a band of 6 or 6.5 get me admission in less competitive fields in some universities of US , Canada, UK ,Aus etc. If so can u name some?
Answer: IELTS/TOEFL scores are not su much admission criteria in the US as they are rejection criteria. In other words, if your scores are particularly low, many institutions will not consider you for admission, but merely meeting the expected score (or even being well above that score) will not help your admission case. You absolutely can get admitted to many American universities, because there are a number that accept all student who have completed their secondary education. The operative question is this: how much can you afford? Figure a starting cost of $30,000 a year; the more you can afford, the more choices you will have. A higher score on an English exam may open more of these institutions, but you will not get much below that price.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Which bachelor's degree would be better, economics or Computer Science? What are the future career prospects of these degrees?
Answer: Obviously, computer science is better, because it’s far more interesting and important. The fact that I’m a computer science professor should not be interpreted as implying that I’m biased in this. OK, I’m completely biased. You need to study what motivates you to work hard, because it’s that hard work, that intellectual growth, that makes you competitive for white-collar careers. As an aside, Ed is absolutely incorrect; it’s not a gamble. Too many students ignore what they are told to do, which is get involved in career planning. That’s the gamble. Just as you wouldn’t go to class to satisfy your hunger (go to cafeteria), you shouldn’t go to class to plan a career. Do that at the career center.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I need help! Should I get a masters degree in business psychology or in data analytics?
Answer: No. You should find a career that you want to pursue. If that career specifically requires one of these two degrees, and there is sufficient demand in the career and high enough pay to justify pursuing the degree, then go for that degree. Otherwise, graduate school is too expensive and too time-consuming to just pick a degree and hope that it leads to something good.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Should I transfer universities?
Answer: I’m not sure why I was asked to answer this question. It was written seven years ago by a student considering transferring from UIUC to UC Santa Barbara or another West Coast institution. (This information is in a comment.) I can only give you my general response: avoid transferring if possible. There are legitimate reasons to transfer. If you started at a community college and you want to finish a bachelors degree, you probably have to transfer. It’s built into the model. If you decide to pursue a major that your institution doesn’t offer, you probably have to transfer. If your financial situation changes dramatically, it may be beneficial to transfer. But generally speaking, transfers take time, energy, and money, and offer little benefit. You restart life with no social foundation and many transfer students never completely overcome this. You have missed out on many opportunities for career preparation and building your social/professional network. Taking extra terms to complete courses is common. In addition, the original person was proposing leaving an in-state institution for an out-of-state institution, easily doubling or potentially traveling their cost.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What is it like to advocate for veganism, animal rights, and environmentalism as part of the Japanese study abroad program and JET Program in Japan?
Answer: Mark, I scrolled through some of your recent questions, and I see two possibilities. First, you are a troll (which I think unlikely), and second, you have some serious objections to… pretty much everything you’ve looked at in your questions. You seem obsessed with Asian popular culture (which is fine), but then you also seem to want to go into institutions, organizations, and countries, and impose a particular set of political, social, and ethical/moral belief onto the people you encounter. That’s… that’s not why people study abroad. You study abroad to learn, not to teach. Sure, you would be teaching English, but when you hear people say “I learned so much more than I taught“, they’re not being insincere. If you want to be surrounded by people with identical social and political beliefs, there are a number of colleges and universities in the United States that are filled with students (or if not filled with, there are plenty of them) who will share most of your beliefs. If you want to experience new things with an openness that will allow you to both enjoy your experiences and grow personally, study abroad. If you can’t go in with that mindset, don’t study abroad. Are there people in Japan who are vegetarian? Sure. Are there vegans? Well, veganism is a western idea not only encompasses not only how people eat, but why they eat that way, but I’m sure you’ll find some vegans. I’m equally certain that if you try to project those values, you won’t have a good experience and you won’t have as many opportunities to learn. By all means, continue your own eating habits. But if you go to Japan, let the Japanese do as they see fit.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Have any of you became successful without university? I just got rejected because I missed entry requirements by one grade and need some hope stories.
Answer: You don’t need hope stories. Hope stories are fantasies that you can replicate what somebody else did. Maybe you can and maybe you can’t, but wishful thinking won’t make it so. What you need is a plan. Absolutely, people become successful without university. It happens all the time. There are also people who go to university and aren’t successful (or at least aren’t particularly successful). However, the education and credential mean that more people who have university degrees are successful (along most reasonable metrics) than people who don’t. But all of that is irrelevant, because for now, it seems that university is not an option for you. OK, so you need a plan, but what does a plan look like? Well, I see two obvious choices. First, there may be a pathway to resolve the grade issue for the next academic year. Second, you can pursue a career pathway that does not involve university. Many European countries have extensive vocational training programs. Some have professional apprenticeship programs. In the United States, we have trade and vocational schools. You may be able to start a full-time job without any training or education, but these jobs usually don’t pay well and offer limited future growth opportunities. As somebody who came close to but didn’t quite make it into university, that’s probably not a good fit. Some people think that I’m particularly harsh when I make statements like this, but I have a reason for doing it: you need to be shocked into action. You hopefully already know that people are successful without university. You might not know many people like that, but that doubles the reason why you need to be shocked into action. I do have sympathy for you. Coming close to achieving something and not getting it sucks. I know that because life is full of failures. Your life is not defined by failure, but by what you do after. I failed many things, but sooner or later I have looked past what I failed at and toward what I can do, and then moved forward. Not only have those actions defined my life much more than my failures, but the sooner I have moved on to something new, the happier I have been. So take your time, lick your wounds, find ways to be happy in the short term, but sooner rather than later, you need to figure out what your options are and choose one of them to act upon.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Why do US universities charge tuition fees for an optional paper in an MS?
Answer: If completing the paper or thesis or whatever it is requires you to register for a course, you will pay tuition for that course. For the last semester of my PhD, I chose to not take an assistantship so that I could write full time. I had to pay (IIRC) $1500 to register for zero credits. I was registered for a course that counted as zero credits, and it cost me $1500. What did I get for that money? The ability to defend my thesis and complete my degree (along with access to the library and other resources).

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Are ACC as level results okay? I need an A*BB to get into the uni I want, however, I get 2 grade reductions from my pathway. I’m on track to get an A* in my math.
Answer: Probably not ok, but why not simply ask the university?

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: What are the best university majors for employment in the US over the next 10 years?
Answer: Majors aren't employment. Jobs and careers are employment. Majors are only loosely connected to careers; there are exceptions, like nursing and engineering, but those are the exceptions, not the rule. The most important thing for you to do is find an academic subject in which you can really push yourself, work very hard, and excel. It's the work that's valuable, the effort, the growth you experience, not the major. Alongside that, you need to get involved in career planning and preparation, and you need to do that from the start, not six months before you graduate. That's why I was able to launch a career in software development having majored in English. You might think, "OK, but that's just you." Nope. My roommate? English major, became a software developer.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I want to go to the same college as all of my sisters since it’s cheap and in state, but they only offer associates, and I’d like to get my forensics bachelors. Is it worth transferring schools 2 years in?
Answer: In really general terms, transferring is fine. Associate of arts and associate of science (AA or AS) degrees are set up with transferring in mind (but not AAS). However transfering is not a perfect system. You will miss out on some opportunities that you would have gotten if you started at a four-year institution. In addition, it's not uncommon to see students take longer than a total of four years to complete their bachelor's degree as a consequence of having started at a community college. Even taking one extra year negates the cost savings in the long run. Community colleges are sometimes treated as a sort of generic resource with no identity or particular qualities, and I think that that's mistaken. Exist to serve specific groups of students, and if it's a good fit for you, then you should go. If it's not a good fit for you you shouldn't. the only way to really find out is to visit both community college and a couple of four year colleges in your area. It is great to go to public, in-state colleges and universities; the costs are generally much lower. You do have more options than just one community college; your state will have multiple four-year institutions. You need to figure out what these are, anyway; these will be your choices for transferring when you complete your associate's degree.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: I have graduated with a BA but need to retake 3 classes I got B-'s in so I can get accepted into a master’s program. Would I be eligible for financial aid through FAFSA?
Answer: First, William is correct; there is no reason to take these three classes unless some graduate program has specifically told you to retake them. In fact, retaking the might not even help you. Second, FAFSA is a form. Perhaps that's clear to you, but perhaps not. FAFSA doesn't decide your eligibility, it just lets you figure out your eligibility. I can tell you without FAFSA what you're eligible for: federal Direct loans. That's it. And possibly not very much; there's an absolute cap of $31,000 for dependent students. And that's not per year or per degree; that's total for all undergraduate coursework, and regardless of whether or not you have paid back those loans. Beyond that, you either have to look at private loans or ask your parents to take out Parent PLUS loans. If you will be an independent student, you can take out more and take your own PLUS loans (although private loans are usually better than plus loans). Theoretically, you could get institutional aid from a public college or university, but most postbacc students get nothing; institutions focus their aid on first-degree students. If a private college or university wants you as a student, they will offer you a standard discount, which is about 50% off tuition. It's usually still significantly more expensive than a comparable institution.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Do I have enough extracurriculars? I am a high school sophomore I am taking Computer Science Pathways and Math 3 and last year I took Math 2 I am in the Cross country team and Track team in school, but I am not that good I have 3 Bs
Answer: If you are a solid B plus student, with a an unweighted GPA somewhere between 3.25 and 3.5, you should focus on doing as well as possible in your academic work. If you enjoy being on running teams, continue doing that, but don't do it just because you hope that it's going to get you into somewhere. Given your math course names, I assume you are in California. For admission to California public universities, only your sophomore and junior year grades count; there's actually a system for determining the GPA that both University of California and California State University schools will use. In other words, none of the grades you've earned so far count either four or against you. You should focus on bringing your GPA up by learning the material better. Assuming one of those grades was on math too, it seems like you weren't placed correctly; it's actually worse to take an accelerated class if you can't do as well as you could have done on the regular class. Let's look at a hypothetical scenario. Let's say you graduate with a GPA of 3.4 (unweighted), and that using the/CSU A-G weighted GPA calculation, you have a 3.7. You will not really be competitive for most University of California schools, or poor Cal Poly SLO. Some additional extra credit activities won't change that. If you are capable of running track at the D1 level, sure, but you probably aren't. [That's not a criticism of you; very few athletes could ever compete at the D1 level.) The single largest group of college-bound students in California will attend CSU schools. I realize that's disappointing to a lot of students, but not everybody is going to get into a UC, and that's by design. Some students start at community colleges in the hope of getting to a UC school, but most won't succeed. Again, the system is designed for that. Running is great. I love running, although I've never been particularly competitive. If you enjoy being on the teams, continue. Having an additional activity will actually help you manage time better, and there are physical and mental health benefits to being very active. But remember that school is primarily about learning, and that your goal is knowledge not extracurricular activities, and not even getting admitted to particular universities.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Does school prestige matter in the field of engineering? If so, to what extent?
Answer: Does it matter? Sure. If you have a degree in mechanical engineering from MIT, it won't be hard to get interviews. If you compare that to somebody with a degree from Podunk State University, they will have to work harder on networking to open doors. If you're not near big city, a degree from MIT is something of a novelty; MIT grads can get interviews just because, "hey , why not interview this person?" MIT grads will have a large number of highly successful people in their network already, and if those folks have a higher opinion of someone, finding jobs will certainly be easier. However, no degree is magic. The world is not so full of exceptional people that engineers with drive and skill can easily be ignored, regardless of where they got their degree. Someone with a degree from Podunk State might have to do a bit more networking and a bit more hustling, but once you're in a job, nobody really cares when your degree is from. I can also assure you that people with degrees MIT are routinely turned down for engineering jobs. there's another problem: what is prestige? It's not something measurable, and it's very subjective. I know people who have bad experiences with grads from specific programs, and their impression of the program is largely driven by those experiences. I don't know if those experiences are atypical or not, but it doesn't really matter; my point is that prestige is complicated, and no institution has a lock on it. If you can get into a place like MIT, or a public flagship research university in your state, or an otherwise highly competitive engineering program, and you feel like it's a good fit, and it's reasonably affordable, you should go. There's no reason to go to Podunk State you have other options that could potentially help your career. But don't think that where you earn your degree will decide your future. You decide your future with what you do.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Has anyone ever had their PhD research proposal rejected only for the prospective supervisor to use the idea for themselves or their current students?
Answer: I don't know of specific instances of this happening, but PhD advisors are human beings, and some of them are quite crappy human beings. Obviously, no advisor should do this, but I would be genuinely stunned if it had never happened in the history of higher education in the United States.(I can't speak of higher education outside of the US because I don't have enough knowledge, but I have no reason to believe that it's dramatically better.) I do recall a story from grad school; I hung out with some math PhD students, and one of them had been working on a proof that would have been a core part of his dissertation. One weekend his advisor solved it, and he had to go back and start over again with a new problem. I don't know why the advisor did this, but it was not intentional cruelty (from what I could see).

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: How do you connect roads? I've been thinking about Route 66 a lot and how it's broken up into sections. What would one have to do in order to restore it and make it drivable again?
Answer: I just want to draw attention to Jim Grupé's answer to How do you connect roads? I've been thinking about Route 66 a lot and how it's broken up into sections. What would one have to do in order to restore it and make it drivable again? The original US highways were literally routes, a set of directions over existing roads. These routes were marked with route markers, which basically said, "you are on Route 66" and "turn here to get/stay on Route 66." As you drove Route 66 into Carlinville, IL, you'd be on North Broad Street, but at the town square, you'd look around to West Main. (Or, of course, the reverse.) Except when you didn't. Because these were literally just routes down existing roads, they could and did change. Why? Sometimes to deal with traffic, sometimes to take advantage of improved roads, and sometimes for political reasons; having Route 66 go through your town would bring drivers who would spend money. Eventually, money was spent at the state and national level to improve roadways and even sometimes to pave new roads, but all of that became irrelevant in the face of the national highway system (the Interstate highways). These were largely federally funded, and a lot of new roadway was paved. In many cases, whole neighborhoods were destroyed to make way for the interstates. The old US highways became relics, because no one would go down them unless specifically interested. The routes were officially integrated with the interstates where possible and now mostly exist as gaps or extensions of interstates. Some, like Route 66, no longer officially exist, but of course roadways have not generally been closed or removed. For some of these routes, including Route 66, organizations have created unofficial maps showing how to navigate as much of the route as possible, including showing variations that existed at different times.

Question: Do adjunct professors work outside of class days? I will be teaching a Monday-Wednesday class this semester, and I currently have another job where I work Tuesdays, Thursdays and the weekend.
Answer: It seems as though you are teaching a single course. Assuming that it is a course you are familiar with (ideally have talked before), you are not creating new curriculum) the school is giving you existing curriculum to teach, including assignments, etc.), and you have Good habits/experience with grading work, responding to student emails, and dealing with other issues, it's reasonable to assume you will get your work done on these two days. In addition, you rarely have a commitment about when you're doing this work, although there may be rules about responding to student emails in a timely manner and/or having office hours (which can usually be done online). If this is a new course for you, the content is unfamiliar, you have to build the curriculum as you're going, and/or you don't have good time management and focus skills with things like grading, you will be stunned at the amount of time it will take you to get this work done.

Question: What are any healthcare programs that I can take fully online only for two years? My ideal goal was to become a radiology tech, but I can't find any online programs to enroll in that only requires 2 years. If anyone know please send recommendations!

Question: Can I do a master’s in the US without doing a postgraduate if I have 123 US credit bachelor's but it is only of 3 years not 4 years? Will the university accept it?
Answer: In American higher education, we don't have something labeled "a postgraduate"; postgraduate (or more commonly just graduate or grad) program or school refers to all degrees earned after undergraduate education, so master's degrees and doctorates. You may be thinking of postbaccalaureate studies, often abbreviated as postbacc, which is coursework completed after a bachelor's degree, but not enrolled in a graduate program, and not necessarily graduate-level coursework Broadly speaking, the question is not how long it took you to complete or how many credits you took, but what degree you earned and its equivalency in the United States. In some countries, there are (for lack of a better word) lesser bachelor's degrees offered in addition to traditional bachelor's degrees. The former often can be completed in less time than the latter. The two most common bachelor's degrees in the US are the bachelor of arts and the bachelor of science. In India, these same labels are used for degrees that are often completed in less time than the more popular options in engineering and commerce and are generally NOT equivalent to the same degrees in the US, even if they use the same labels. However, some are generally considered equivalent to US bachelor's degrees based on both the student's performance and the rating of the institution. The unofficial authority on this is the World Education Service, which (among other things) reviews transcripts from around the world and produces reports that applicants send to US colleges and universities.[1] In the UK, students start a bachelor's degree course having already completed some preparatory coursework, so while UK bachelor's degrees typically take three years, they are equivalent to US four-year bachelor's degrees. However, programs that offer a higher national diploma (HND) or equivalent are not considered bachelors degrees. To simplify, you really just need to contact WES. They should be able to provide you with general outlines before you actually submit your paperwork. Before you begin, you should know that it can be very expensive to earn a masters degree in the United States. It will typically take two years, and when you combine living expenses, tuition fees, and mandatory health insurance, you should expect to spend at least $40,000 a year. You cannot work enough in the United States to offset most of that cost. You will have to have one year of costs in hand before being given a student visa.

Question: A judge has ruled that UCLA can’t allow pro-Palestinian students to block Jews from entering the campus. Why was UCLA defending such actions to the point where the courts had to order UCLA to not defend racism?
Answer: UCLA was not defending the actions of the pro-Palestinian students; they were saying that these students were acting independently, not as agents of the university. In other words, they were saying that they didn't have a responsibility to get into the middle of a dispute between two groups of students, even when it was clear which students were the aggressors, and it was clear that these "protestors" were violating the civil rights of the victims. UCLA obviously does have such a responsibility, and that's why they lost. The judge additionally ordered UCLA to create a plan to defend the rights of Jewish students on campus. So let's be clear, UCLA was not "defending racism" in the sense that they were attempting to advocate for these pro-Palestinian protesters. UCLA was trying to abdicate its responsibility to protect a group of students. Still a pretty awful thing to do, but different than what you described. As for why UCLA wasn't acting responsibly, they claimed that they were trying to avoid escalation. They aren't lying, but it's not really an excuse.

Question: Can I study general engineering program in community college then transfer my credits to university to study petroleum engineering?
Answer: You can, but it may not be a great idea and may not work well. First, I would just assume that it will take more than four years, which sort of negates the possible financial advantage of attending community college. Second, a majority of engineering students transfer to other majors, and you want to figure that out earlier (again, with an eye to finishing in a timely manner). Third, there aren’t that many petroleum engineering programs, and I would have to assume that they are competitive. You need to establish now what’s expected to be admitted as a transfer student. Ideally, there would be an actual articulation agreement for petroleum engineering, or at least for the college of engineering. This is different than course articulation; it’s an actual program/plan that will get you through the whole degree. I’d be surprised if there was one specific to petroleum engineering, just because it’s an uncommon major. I’m a big supporter of community colleges, but they aren’t the universally appropriate choice. They are one option, and for the right student, they are an excellent option. For students who aren’t a good fit, they create more problems than advantages (which is true of every college university).

Question: As a PhD student, if you intend to drop out and pursue job opportunities, should you leave out your PhD from your resume because someone currently pursuing a PhD may be less likely to get job offers due to their commitment to studies?
Answer: As Barbara indicates, including it (along with a clear indication that you have stopped pursuing the program and that you did not complete the degree) shows that you are capable of hard work and focus, and its presence eliminates a need to explain a significant gap. Some people worry about coming off as “stiff“ or “overly academic“, but at that point you are playing a guessing game about what other people want and how they perceive you, and it’s just an exercise and frustration. Over time, you may remove it from your résumé, or simply listed as graduate level coursework.

Question: How important are A-level grades in the USA and the UK?
Answer: In the UK, A-level grades determine your admission to university. In the US, they don’t exist as part of our education system. British applicants to American colleges and universities can submit them, and they may play a large role in admission. They may also qualify students to receive credit for or not be required to take certain classes.

Question: Why do a lot of teenagers at elite Prep Schools think they know everything the guest speakers are talking about, when they have 0 experience in the field? Was it like this before the internet?
