It may well be annoying, but it’s usually not really all that important. And there’s nothing new about this. It’s a bit easier to find general information, but people did this before the internet and before social media. Unless it’s directly creating problems for you, just let it go. They have their own paths to follow, and their own challenges.

Question: What are my chances of getting into UMD aerospace engineering with a 1470 SAT and a 3.75 GPA?
Answer: Why do people rarely give us the information we need? Two questions: As I’m sure you’re aware, the GPA is weak if it’s unweighted. If that’s a weighted GPA, it’s very alarming. Question: Instead of going to an American high school, does going to a Canadian high school have any disadvantages/problems when trying to go to top American universities(or even not the top American universities)?

Question: Is it possible to apply to the PhD finance program in the USA with a GRE score of 281?

Question: What is a community college in Jacksonville, Florida which doesn't require high grades?
Answer: Generally speaking, community colleges only require that you complete high school or a GED. However, that will not make you eligible for competitive programs. If you want to be a nurse, for example, you will need to complete at least a year of college-level prerequisites (often with very high grades) to be admitted to an associate of science in nursing (ASN) degree program. Most community colleges offer or require placement tests. You should take them and follow the recommendations. If they suggest repeating a course you took in high school, you should do so. Just because you passed a class doesn’t mean you have retained enough of the information and skills to be able to use what you learned. In addition, you must earn passing grades to graduate and transfer to a four-year college or university. The better your grades, the more choices you will have of where to transfer to, and it may impact how much you pay.

Question: Suppose I took German 1 sophomore year, then took German 2 and German 3 in junior year, and then IB SL German in senior year. Would this count as 4 years of language credits?

One option would be a summer program, and another would be to see if you could do third and fourth semester German in dual enrollment in your senior year of high school. if you can, I would strongly encourage you to look for summer programs, especially study abroad programs, but they can be expensive.

Question: I am starting college (a top school) at 22 and feeling old. A lot happened after high school so I had to postpone it even though I want a STEM degree so much. How weird is it to graduate at 25-26?
Answer: I'm going to be blunt: it's going to feel very weird at first. Most of your classmates (especially at a very competitive institution) are almost certainly going to be 18 or 19 years old, and at your present age, that age gap is significant. It's more profound if a lot of things have happened in your life over the past three or four years. However, that feeling will rapidly disappear. It won't be noticeable very much in your sophomore year, and by the time you graduate, it's just not going to matter very much. You just have to get through that initial discomfort. And note that I wrote that it will feel weird. Just because something feels weird doesn't mean that it is weird. Your only other choice would be to skip your goals, which would be kind of foolish, right? I suspect that if you look, you will find other people your age, and knowing even one or two other people your age will make you more comfortable. Beyond that, realize that it actually is fine to interact with and even socialize with 18-year-olds. I think there are some potential boundary concerns, but you aren't so old as to have little in common with your classmates.

Question: I'm going into my senior year in high school. If I got mediocre grades the first 3 years, can I still get a scholarship or even get into college if I dedicate myself to working extra hard this year?

Question: It does not say of their website. Or I have not found it yet. Does anyone know the required GPA to get accepted to a DMA program at Yale ISM?

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Does a top secret military aircraft become declassified only when it reaches obsolescence?
Answer: What? No. It depends a bit on what kind of declassification you’re talking about, but no. Programs in the US become declassified (that is, the aircraft’s existence is acknowledged) when it’s in the interest of the government or when they just can’t deny it anymore. Most aircraft, even quite secretive aircraft in terms of how they are built, are acknowledged very early on, because intimidation is a useful longterm tool in diplomacy. It’s also helpful politically to look serious about defense, to get support for big budgets, and be seen as creating job opportunities. The most secretive aircraft program in recent decades was the F-117. Its design predecessor, Have Blue, first flew in 1977. The F-117 first flew in 1981. It’s a bit unclear when the Soviets became aware of it, but it was a secret program and not generally, publicly known of. The first (known) use of the F-117 was in the invasion of Panama in 1989. In the Gulf War in 1991, it became well-known. At that point, knowledge of the aircraft was declassified. An F-117 was shot down in 1999 (and another was hit by a missile), and it was not deployed to actively-contested theaters after that (AFAIK). We could call that obsolescence. Since then, a great deal of information has been declassified, but I’m sure that some information about it is still classified. While the A-12 and YF-12 had already flown, the existence of the SR-71 Blackbird was acknowledged before it flew. The aircraft programs that led to the F-22 and F-35 were public before the prototype competitions were held. The B-21 hasn’t flown yet (AFAIK), but we know basic specs. Aircraft generally aren’t kept secret. However, there is certainly a great deal of information about aircraft like the F-11, the F-35, and the B-21 that is classified.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: Is it true that the strength of UC Berkeley's Computer Science program is mostly due to its graduate division?

I don’t put universities or departments on pedestals; there are other excellent programs in California, even ones that surprise some people. And outcomes are not based on program “quality”; they’re individual. But Berkeley has a long and well-earned reputation as an exceptional CS program at all levels.

Question: How can I get into UC Berkeley for a master’s in CS as a bachelor mathematics student at UIO from Norway?
Answer: It’s a very competitive program. It’s also primarily designed for students who want to get into PhD programs (so it has strong research emphasis). The UC Berkeley MS CS is a stretch/reach program for ALL candidates. It should be one of several programs you apply to, and there should be less-competitive programs in the list, too.

Name: Joshua Gross
Question: If my sponsor lives & works at a US government company, is it an advantage, will that help me go to US?
Answer: For an F-1 visa, you do not need an advantage. Many things that people consider to be advantages can actually be disadvantages. You need to demonstrate that you have sufficient funding to pay for your education, that you have a strong commitment to return home, and that you will not create problems (e.g, commit crimes) while in the US. That's it. F-1 visas are not competitive; the US will grant all of them that meet the standard of demonstrating all three things. Most (a significant majority) F-1 visas applications are granted. I think the biggest misunderstanding that people have about the process (and I write this as an outsider who has never gone through the process, but I've had many students who have) is the assumption that it's an adversarial process. This creates two problems. First, applicants go in with a defensive attitude, and second, they wait for challenges. The visa officer is not going to challenge you; they're just going to ask you questions. It is your job to demonstrate the things I've listed above.

Question: If I have an engineering degree from a US school, but get a masters in Europe and want to move back to the US, will my masters degree still help me or not be as valid?
Answer: Because of ABET rules, very few master's degree programs in engineering are actually accredited; ABET does not allow programs to offer both accredited bachelor's and master's degrees (the program must choose which degree receives accreditation).[1] EDITED TO ADD: As Jeff Erickson points out below, ABET removed the “one accredited program” rule years ago, but few master’s degree programs are accredited. He links a paper that offers some insight into why; basically, the rules are vague and offer limited value for a program. At the time of publication in 2020, ten US and seven international master’s degree programs were accredited. Assuming your bachelor's degree is from an accredited program, that's good news. Not all engineering careers require accreditation/PE/FE, but if your field requires or prioritizes those, they may be beneficial or necessary. The problem with pursuing a degree in Europe is that you will not be connected to the US job market. Your network will not be as strong as it would be if you had pursued a masters degree in the US. If you have a strong network from your undergraduate degree, that shouldn't matter too much.

Question: Do we get certifications, degrees, and career guidance for professional advancement obtained from educational institutions?
Answer: The primary value of educational institutions is (unsurprisingly) education, which is the improved ability to learn and make use of knowledge. However, all colleges and universities in the United States have career centers that offer extensive support for career preparation, entry, and advancement. Relatively few students take make any use of them, and if they do, they tend to go right at the end, shortly before they graduate (raises hand). The time to go is when you're starting college, so you can figure out a career plan, including choosing a career to move toward. Your career and your major are often not connected; very few careers expect a specific major. Then you need to keep going back to advance your career plan. As for certifications, some academic programs are tied to licensure, but the licensure would come from the state. Similarly, some colleges may offer preparation for certificates from private companies. /Certification are very valuable, and ins so they are utterly worthless. Do not assume that a certificate is by itself significant career preparation. Colleges and universities are authorized to grant degrees, and a degree is a demonstration of continued academic work along particular path. How valuable that degree is will depend on how committed you were to the education, experiential learning, and career prep associated with your chosen career.

Question: What are the rankings of Penn State for data science programs?
Answer: I don't know and neither should. Rankings aren't important Assuming you like the program and can afford it, it's going to be good and lead to good outcomes. You need to understand a little bit about the history of IST in order to understand why. In the late 1990s, Pennsylvania was experiencing a brain drain, with young people weaving the state rapidly. At one point, it was I believe the second oldest state (having the second highest average age) Florida. That's bad, because old people tend to retire and then use a lot of public resources, rather than start businesses and pay taxes and otherwise contribute to growth. The Governor of Pennsylvania and the President of Penn State got together and said, "these computer things look like they're going to stick around for a while." They wanted to expand computing programs and make them a bit more applied. Supposedly, they offered a fortune to the computer science and engineering department, who refused to create new programs. Instead, the governor and president started the (then School, now College) of Information Sciences and Technology. They brought in a lot of senior faculty, a lot of state money, and a lot of donor money. The focus of the program was always going to emphasize professional success. That isn't to say that the scholarly work done in the program isn lightweight, but from the start, the program had staff who could and did work aggressively to give students great job opportunities, and the programs encouraged skills that would lead to professional success. Each spring, there is a career fair with recruiters from companies who wouldn't normally come to rural Pennsylvania. They aren't recruiting computer science students; they are recruiting IST students specifically. These tend to be more consultant companies than "top tech "companies , but still students had fantastic job opportunities. i'm not saying you should go to Penn State. You need to visit and decide if it's appropriate for you. You also need to consider the cost; Penn State is routine one of the most expensive public universities for in-state students, and it's outrageous for out-of-state students. However, if you decide that it's a good fit for you, you shouldn't worry about outcomes. People don't hire rank; they hire students who demonstrates skills, and IST is excellent at emphasizing demonstration. As you might guess, I have a connection with the program; it's where I did my PhD. You might think that would bias me to be supportive, but the opposite is true. The grand total number of people I've encouraged to do a PhD there is zero. I have very mixed feelings about the program, but those won't really impact you.

Question: Can I teach at a community college one night a week?
Answer: The answer is a strict maybe. First, do you have skills that the community college wants to teach, along with the required/preferred credentials? Ideally you have some professional experience and at least a master's degree in your field. Second, do they have openings? In some fields, community colleges have far more willing instructors than they have courses to offer. If not, do you have a special background sufficient to get them to offer something new? At Blackburn College (admittedly not a community college), a local judge was willing to teach, and to avoid conflict of interest, didn't accept pay from the college. In that kind of situation, the college can and will tend to make accommodations. Third, does the community college already offer once-a-week night courses in your field? Fourth, community colleges tend to let Faculty choose their preferred schedule by seniority, so do they need faculty for those specific classes? In general, it's unusual for a new faculty member to be able to dictate terms, but it's not outside of the realm of possibility. You should definitely contact your local community colleges. I would recommend reaching out to department chairs directly. In another question, you asked about pay. It looks like you're in Utah. Pay is dictated by the community college based on state rules and any union that might exist for the faculty. In Utah, I assume there is no union. I've seen pay in recent years as low as $1800 for a single course. People don't teach at community college if their primary goal is to make money. Assuming 10 hours of work a week, you're making the equivalent of $12 an hour, and 10 hours is probably underestimating the commitment, especially at first.

Question: Why is P=NP's description in computer science different than physics description of everything being connected?
Answer: I'm not really sure I understand the question, but I will hazard a guess. In physics, one goal is the "theory of everything" that (in theory) connects all physical phenomena, including particles and forces, but also integrating relatively and quantum theory. The goal is to tie together everything in physics, because there's a general belief that in physics, everything must be connected to everything else. We have no equivalent in computer science. P=NP is a really important open question in the theory of computation. If the answer is that P does equal NP, that's going to impact a lot of things. But it's not something that most of us concern ourselves with every day. In fact, except for a couple of somewhat oblique references in a course, I don't think about it at all. If there is a concept closer to the heart of computer science, it's the general concept of computability. Even that isn't something we think about daily. Computer science is a formal science rather than a natural science. It isn't a description of a world that exists outside of human experience; it's a world that exists within human mind, and that we can model using machines that can exist in the physical world. Because there's no external reality to computer science, there's no belief, need, or even value to a theory of everything.

Question: As a university admin or dept. head, how do you manage course registration in a way to ensure that all students get necessary/chosen sections/teachers & class-times and yet, all sections of each course get a similar number of students?
Answer: The first priority of a department chair (with respect to registration) is to ensure that qualified instructors are in place for all courses on sequence. In the United States, catalogs will list which semesters/terms a given course is offered, and it's generally problematic if courses aren't offered in terms in which they are supposed to. Their second goal is to ensure that there are enough seats for all students who need the course. After that, everything they might accomplish is less important. Speaking bluntly, administrators above the department level often don't really care about this. In my own institution, in fact in my own program, administrators are admitting students even today. Courses start in just over two weeks. We don't have seats for these students this semester, and we definitely don't have seats for them next semester. The administration is hoping that students will leave computer science for other (heavily undersubscribed) and that my department chair will be able to magically find qualified instructors for additional sections. They have not offered her any support or resources to do this, or additional support for our classes that have high enrollment. I have 10 TA hours to spread across two sections of 40 students each.

Question: If I have a convincing reason for not taking SAT exam, and I email the university, is there any likelihood to get admission? Or if I apply for a university that SAT is optional should I tell them my reason?
Answer: Regardless of what you write, if you don't submit your SAT scores, the college or university will assume that you don't have high scores relative to the range from which they normally admit. Perhaps because you didn't take the SAT, and perhaps because you took it and did not score well. The only exception to this would be at institutions that are test blind, like the University of California or California State University system schools. Is it possible to get around taking the SAT? Maybe. A friend of mine with a rather profound physical disability was admitted to a PhD program without taking the GRE back when the GRE was required for most PhD programs in my field, and certainly for this program). Disability would've made taking the GRE difficult, and it prevented him from applying more broadly to PhD programs. They knew if they admitted him, he would accept. Buy PhD programs are special; the number of applicants is dramatically smaller, and they have been vetted in other ways. I saw a post on Reddit last night in a r/civilengineering. (I have no idea why I follow that subreddit.) Anyway, a manager was posting about a remote summer intern of theirs who refused to make the drive from Boston to New York for a day. The purpose of the day was to give the intern some on-site experience. His objection was that he was not used to driving long distances and that his parents wouldn't allow him. He is apparently 20 years old. Now this kid is not going to lose their job and won't get a bad reference or anything. However, it brings up a potentially very important point: what you perceive as a good reason may not match what a college or university perceives as a good reason. For example, I've seen students say, "I can't take the SAT; I get test anxiety." Having test anxiety doesn't mean you can't take the SAT. It means potentially challenging factors, but it doesn't mean that you can't take the SAT. People have had anxiety for a long, long time, and countless of them have taken the SAT, even (I assure) this year. I think you owe it to yourself to think about how refusals like this are perceived by people. It looks like you are unwilling to step out of your comfort zone. It looks like you would rather give up than take a risk. This is not a good look. I won't be surprised if I get blasted for telling people to torment themselves or whatever, but I don't really care. In your heart, you must know that I'm not wrong about how people perceive things.

Question: What is life like for a student-athlete in college?
Answer: It’s going to depend. If you are a scholarship athlete in a marquee sport, your sport will dominate your life during the season. You may primarily or exclusively socialize with others in your sport. The athletic department may pick your courses, and at least some athletics departments in the past have also arranged for someone else to do your work. Then you either run out your eligibility or you graduate. Hopefully the latter. The odds of you going pro are not much better than someone who is not in your sport. Or you might play a sport life golf at a university like Cal State Monterey Bay. I’ve had multiple golfers, soccer players, and volleyball players. They’re busy, but not insanely so. Because of practice, training, and events I have had more than one quit their sport at some point in their academic career so that they could focus on schoolwork, career prep, and/or a job search. They have friends who aren’t on their team, but they do tend to spend a fair bit of time with other athletes. Or you might play a club sport. We have a club water polo team. Club teams compete with club teams from other institutions, but it’s relatively casual and mostly about fun. As a result, students on these teams tend to have fewer commitments.

Question: I’m going to take the full International Baccalaureate program, but want to take a few AP courses as well. What courses would you recommend so credits/content doesn’t overlap?
Answer: AP and IB have something significant in common: they allow students to specialize. Obviously, IB is more extensive, since it’s a whole baccalaureate program, not an a la carte menu of courses like AP. Even so, the overlap will depend on what you choose to take. This is a discussion to have with your counselor. We don’t know what you plan to take or even what your options are.

Question: I’m a high school student working toward becoming a radiation therapist. Is taking college level statistics worth it (dual enrollment)?
Answer: Yes, absolutely, taking college statistics will be worthwhile. You will likely need to complete either an associate’s degree or a bachelor’s degree, and it’s highly likely that a course of this type will be required or help count toward general education and/or admission to the program. Programs are typically competitive, and every health field deals with statistical data.

Question: Do scholarships automatically disqualify you if you have a lot in savings from your FASFA account. If I’m aiming for a merit based scholarship, And they require a fafsa submission will they check my overall assets or parents income?
Answer: OK, there’s no such thing as a “FAFSA account”, at least not in the sense that it’s something that holds money. But I suspect you’re concerned that scholarships may not consider you if you and/or your family have a lot of assets/income listed on your FAFSA. FAFSA gives you a number, the Student Aid Index (SAI). This is an updated version of the old Expected Family Contribution (EFC), but it’s calculated differently. It’s the amount the rules say that you/your family can pay. In addition to the FAFSA, there’s another form, the CSS (College Scholarships Service) offered by the College Board. This costs money to complete, but they have pretty extensive fee waivers. Many institutions require the CSS. There are generally four kinds of aid: If the scholarship requires you to share your FAFSA with them, it may just be to demonstrate that you’re basically eligible for aid (e.g., a US citizens or permanent resident). However, they may restrict the scholarship to or prefer applicants with higher needs. Most scholarships give clear indications of how they decide.

Question: What are my chances of getting into Harvard MD school? 9 rec. letters from doctors, started a successful charity, have my own successful startup, 500+ volunteering hours, 90% average in lifesciences, started my own first aid club in HS.
Answer: Low. Assuming that you have a bachelor’s degree in life sciences, you have taken the MCAT and scored well, and you are either a US citizen or permanent resident, you stand a low chance of getting in. It’s not quite negligible or zero, but it’s not good. If you don’t have that, your chances are nil. And it’s not that Harvard has the best medical school. It’s just that it’s Harvard. Arguably the most famous brand in academia. If they opened an auto repair school, it would be inundated with applications.
